Third, beginning on August 1, 2021, and ongoing, the complainant alleged that she was subjected to micromanagement, was assigned to either the rewrap section or city manual section in a manner suggesting discriminatory intent, and was confronted regarding her job duties.
Fourth, on August 31, 2021, the complainant alleged that her request for a temporary change of schedule was denied in a manner consistent with discriminatory treatment.
## AGENCY INVESTIGATION AND REPORT OF INVESTIGATION

Following completion of its investigation into the complaint, the Agency transmitted a Report of Investigation (ROI) and Notice of Right to Request a Hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) to the complainant and her non-attorney representative on April 5, 2022.

Concurrent with this transmission, the Agency emailed both parties, indicating that an electronic copy of the final ROI would be available for download for a period of thirty days and requesting confirmation of receipt via email.

Documentary evidence in the case file reflects that the message was relayed to the complainant and her representative; however, the destination server did not provide a delivery notification, creating ambiguity regarding actual receipt.
It is noteworthy that the Agency initially accepted a formulation of the coworker verbal abuse allegation that differed from the complainant's original statement.
The Agency's initial framing dated the incident as July 20, 2021, and characterized the alleged abuser as a supervisor rather than a coworker.

During the investigation, the complainant clarified that the incident occurred on July 19, 2021, that it was indeed a coworker (not a supervisor) who engaged in the verbal abuse, and that supervisory personnel failed to take corrective action after she reported the incident.
## ADDITIONAL DOCUMENTS AND AFFIDAVITS

On April 5, 2022, coinciding with transmission of the ROI, the Agency provided the complainant and her representative with additional documents that had been submitted after the completion of the investigative file, requesting that these materials be added to the complainant's copy of the file.
These supplementary documents included an investigative affidavit from an Acting Supervisor, completed on March 28, 2022, and the Acting Supervisor's Litigation Hold Notice, signed on March 31, 2022.

In this initial affidavit, the Acting Supervisor stated that he maintained no organizational relationship to the complainant during the relevant time period and that he was not present at the facility on July 20, 2021.
On May 17, 2022, the Agency again emailed the complainant and her representative, advising that an electronic copy of the ROI would be available for download for thirty days.
Similar to the prior transmission, the Agency's system indicated that the message was relayed but that the destination server did not provide a delivery notification.
The documentary evidence suggests that materials were ultimately provided via first-class mail.
## COMPLAINANT'S RESPONSE AND HEARING REQUEST
On May 31, 2022, the complainant mailed a formal hearing request to both the Agency and the Commission's New York District Office.
The Agency's stamped records indicate receipt on June 6, 2022.

Accompanying the hearing request was a letter dated May 28, 2022, in which the complainant expressed her intent to refute statements made by the Acting Supervisor in his affidavit, particularly his claim that he was not present on the date of the verbal abuse incident.
The complainant requested that the Agency provide her with the Acting Supervisor's Employee Everything Report to corroborate his presence or absence on that date.
According to the complainant's account, on May 18, 2022, she contacted an EEO Services Analyst to discuss the Acting Supervisor's contradictory statements.
The complainant alleged that the EEO Services Analyst informed her that her case had been closed on May 1, 2022.

When the complainant questioned how her case could be closed without notification or provision of a copy of the ROI, she was reportedly instructed that she could file a hearing request but should attach a letter explaining that she discovered the case closure date of May 18, 2022.
## SUBSEQUENT AGENCY DECISION AND APPEAL
On June 2, 2022, the Agency issued a final decision, citing 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b) as the basis for the decision and asserting that the complainant failed to submit a hearing request within the timeframe specified in 29 C.F.R.
The Agency concluded in its decision that the complainant failed to establish that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged in her complaint.
The EEOC's New York District Office received the complainant's hearing request on June 10, 2022, which was subsequently docketed as Hearing No.
On June 15, 2022, the complainant filed an appeal of the Agency's final decision.
## UPDATED AGENCY AFFIDAVIT AND ADMINISTRATIVE ADJUDICATION
On July 6, 2022, the Agency submitted an updated affidavit from the Acting Supervisor, requesting that this document also be added to the complainant's file.
In this revised affidavit dated June 7, 2022, the Acting Supervisor provided substantially different testimony.
He stated that, during the timeframe of the complaint, his organizational relationship with the complainant was that of Acting Supervisor.

The Acting Supervisor reiterated that he was not present when the coworker verbally abused the complainant on July 19, 2021, and stated that he did not know whether the complainant or anyone acting on her behalf reported the harassment incident.

On November 29, 2022, an EEOC Administrative Judge issued an order dismissing the complainant's hearing request, noting that the Agency had already issued a final decision on the matter, which the complainant had appealed.
# INVESTIGATIVE CASE FILE RECORD
## COMPLAINANT EMPLOYMENT STATUS AND INCIDENT TIMELINE

At the time of the events that precipitated this employment discrimination complaint, the Complainant was employed by the United States Postal Service (Agency) as a Level 1 City Carrier assigned to the Meadow Mesa Station facility located in North Las Vegas, Nevada.
On February 25, 2023, the Complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint with the Agency, alleging unlawful discrimination and harassment based on his age.
According to records, the Complainant was born in 1973, which would have made him approximately 49-50 years old at the time the alleged discriminatory incidents occurred.

The complaint encompasses five distinct incidents occurring between August 30, 2022, and November 2, 2022, each of which the Complainant contends was motivated by discriminatory considerations related to his age.
## CLAIM 1: EMERGENCY PLACEMENT ON AUGUST 30, 2022
### Complainant's Account
In his investigative affidavit, the Complainant provided a detailed narrative of the events leading to his initial Emergency Placement (EP) on August 30, 2022.
According to his account, he approached Supervisor S1 and requested that she sign or initial his request form for Union time.

The Complainant stated that when S1 declined to execute the request immediately, informing him that she would attend to the matter later, he inquired why the signature could not be provided at that moment.
S1 allegedly reiterated that the task would be completed at a later time and instructed him to return to work activities.
The Complainant further stated that Postmaster (PM) then intervened in the conversation, asking what situation was developing.
After the Complainant explained the circumstances, PM inquired whether S1 had issued instructions to return to work.
The Complainant confirmed that she had, and PM then questioned whether the Complainant was refusing to comply with those instructions.
The Complainant denied refusing to work but expressed his desire to understand why he was being held to established policy while S1 apparently was not.
Subsequently, while the Complainant was in the employee locker room, PM allegedly entered and asked why he had not yet left the facility.
PM further questioned what the Complainant had been doing for the preceding hour.
When the Complainant attempted to provide an explanation, he stated that PM interrupted him, raised his voice, and leaned toward him in what the Complainant characterized as an intimidation tactic.
PM then re-entered the locker room and directed the Complainant to deliver mail to apartments that day.

When the Complainant asked whether he needed to complete the apartment delivery, noting that doing so would exceed his eight-hour work limit, PM allegedly accused him of failing to follow instructions, refused his request for union representation, demanded his work badge, yelled at him to remove his personal items from his locker, and threatened to contact law enforcement to have him forcibly removed from the facility.
### Agency Respondents' Accounts

In his affidavit, the Postmaster acknowledged observing the Complainant engaging in what he characterized as time-wasting activities and stated that he issued instructions that the Complainant failed to follow.

The PM asserted that, in accordance with established Agency policy, he placed the Complainant on Emergency Placement in off-duty, non-compensated status due to the failure to follow management instructions.
Regarding the Complainant's allegation of intimidation, the PM characterized the claim as without merit.

He further explained that owing to health considerations following his recovery from COVID-19, he maintains distance from all employees and therefore would not have leaned toward or attempted to intimidate the Complainant.

The PM also addressed the union representation issue, indicating that a union steward was unavailable at the time but that the Complainant was informed he could subsequently speak with his union representative after departing the facility immediately.
Supervisor S1 corroborated elements of the PM's account.
She stated in her affidavit that she had instructed the Complainant approximately three times to proceed with mail delivery, but he did not comply with those directives.
S1 indicated that the Complainant subsequently became argumentative with the Postmaster.
Regarding the intimidation allegation, S1 stated she possessed no knowledge of events that may have transpired in the men's locker room, as she was not present in that location.
She further clarified that Agency policy prohibited employees placed on Emergency Placement from engaging in conversations with union representatives before departing the premises.
### Complainant's Age-Based Theory

The Complainant advanced the theory that his age was a contributing factor in his placement on EP, arguing that he was assigned an overburdened mail route that management expected him to complete within an eight-hour timeframe.
He further alleged that he was subjected to constant unfavorable comparisons with younger carriers.
However, the Complainant could not identify specific examples of younger employees who were similarly situated in all material respects yet received more favorable treatment.
## CLAIM 2: SUSPENSION AND SEATBELT VIOLATION ON SEPTEMBER 14, 2022
### Complainant's Allegations

According to his affidavit, on September 14, 2022, following completion of his vehicle inspection and while loading mail into his assigned truck, Supervisor S2 approached the Complainant and demanded his work badge.

S2 allegedly explained that the Complainant was being removed from the premises because he had not fastened his seatbelt before starting the vehicle and had exited the driver's seat while the engine remained running.
The Complainant stated that he requested union representation, but S2 denied this request.

The Complainant further noted that, according to his understanding, Section 812 of Postal Service Handbook M-41 specified that seatbelts must be worn at all times when a vehicle is in motion, not before the engine is started.
The Complainant was placed on EP in off-duty, unpaid status.

On September 22, 2022, he received a formal Notice of 14-Day Suspension Letter; however, this letter cited the August 30, 2022 failure-to-follow-instructions incident as the rationale for the suspension.
### Supervisor S2's Account
In his affidavit, S2 stated that he observed the Complainant exiting the mail truck and walking in front of the vehicle while its engine was still running.
S2 characterized this conduct as a safety violation and asserted that Agency policy required seatbelts to be worn at all times while operating a vehicle.
S2 explained that because the Complainant was immediately placed on EP, union contact was required to occur off postal property.
### Supervisor S1's Statement
S1 stated she possessed no knowledge of the September 14 incident because she was not present when it occurred.
### Complainant's Age-Based Theory
The Complainant stated that he did not believe his age was a factor in this particular incident.
He also could not provide specific examples of younger employees similarly situated who received more favorable treatment.
## CLAIM 3: BATHROOM INCIDENT AND ALLEGED YELLING ON SEPTEMBER 20, 2022
### Complainant's Allegations
The Complainant alleged that on September 20, 2022, Supervisor S2 followed him into the facility bathroom on two separate occasions and yelled at him.
The Complainant further asserted that S2 threatened him with disciplinary action.
### Supervisor S2's Response
S2 denied raising his voice toward the Complainant.
He stated that if he did follow the Complainant to the bathroom area, such action was warranted based on concerns regarding the Complainant's job performance.

S2 further explained that rather than performing standard hygiene activities, the Complainant appeared to be spending an extended amount of time in the locker room and engaging in unspecified activities at his locker.
### Complainant's Age-Based Theory
The Complainant advanced the theory that his age was a factor in this incident, reasoning that as he has aged, he requires more frequent bathroom breaks than he did during his younger years.
He could not, however, provide specific examples of younger employees treated more favorably under similar circumstances.
## CLAIM 4: SEATBELT POLICY DISPUTE ON SEPTEMBER 24, 2022
### Complainant's Account

On September 24, 2022, the Complainant started his vehicle's engine while fastening his seatbelt when S2 approached the passenger-side window and yelled at him for not having the seatbelt fastened before starting the engine.

The Complainant cited Section 812 of Handbook M-41, arguing that the correct policy required seatbelts to be fastened before the vehicle was shifted into gear and put into motion, not before the engine is merely started.
The Complainant stated that S1 then approached, and S2 asked her whether she observed anything improper.
S1 replied in the negative.
While S1 and S2 engaged in conversation and made telephone calls, the Complainant called the National Association of Letter Carriers (NALC) office.
According to the Complainant, an NALC representative confirmed his interpretation of the Agency's seatbelt policy.
When the Complainant asked to have the NALC officer repeat this confirmation to S1 and S2, S1 stated this was unnecessary.
S1 told the Complainant he could proceed with his mail delivery route.
S1 also instructed him that he must comply with all supervisor instructions and, going forward, must fasten his seatbelt before starting the engine.
### Supervisor S2's Account
S2 stated he believed that seatbelts needed to be fastened before a vehicle is started.
He indicated that he subsequently called the Agency's safety office and was informed that no written Agency policy exists establishing when seatbelts must be fastened.
S2 stated he informed the Complainant of this conversation, after which the Complainant was permitted to proceed to his delivery route.
### Supervisor S1's Account
S1 confirmed that S2 called her over and asked whether she had observed any improper conduct by the Complainant.
S1 stated she did not observe anything wrong.
S1 stated she ultimately directed the Complainant to comply with supervisor instructions.

When asked whether the requirement to fasten seatbelts before starting an engine was applied to all employees going forward, S1 expressed uncertainty, stating she was not sure whether this directive was communicated to all carriers or whether other carriers were already fastening seatbelts before starting their vehicles.
S1 further stated the relevant conversation was between S2 and the Complainant.
### Complainant's Age-Based Theory
The Complainant stated he did not believe his age factored into this incident and could not provide examples of younger employees treated more favorably in similar circumstances.
## CLAIM 5: MEDICAL ACCOMMODATION DENIAL AND REMOVAL ON NOVEMBER 1-2, 2022
### Complainant's Account
On November 1, 2022, the Complainant provided S1 with a physician's note recommending thirty days of no overtime work due to repetitive motion pain affecting his right shoulder.
The Complainant stated that S1 told him she was not obligated to honor the medical documentation.

Later that evening, when the Complainant returned to the facility with undelivered mail and clocked out, S1 allegedly told him he needed to continue delivering mail until completing his assigned route.
When the Complainant reminded S1 of his medical restriction and explained his inability to work overtime, S1 allegedly asked whether he was refusing to follow instructions.

The Complainant stated he responded that he was not obligated to follow instructions he considered unsafe, and that ignoring physician guidance while demanding overtime work did not constitute a safe work practice.
S1 allegedly then demanded his work badge, and he was escorted from the facility.
The Complainant was placed on EP in off-duty, unpaid status, effective November 2, 2022.
### Supervisor S1's Account
S1 provided a different characterization of events.
She stated that the Complainant told her, based on union advice, that he could return his undelivered mail and was not required to listen to management directives.
S1 stated she requested that the Complainant complete his route three times, but he repeatedly reiterated what union counsel had allegedly told him.
S1 explained that while the union could provide guidance, the Complainant remained obligated to follow supervisor instructions.
S1 further explained that she forwarded the Complainant's medical documentation to the Agency's Occupational Health Management (OHM) department for guidance.
According to S1, OHM advised her that the Complainant could complete his delivery route that day.

S1 stated that OHM indicated they were investigating the matter and would provide updated guidance regarding whether the physician's note constituted a limited duty job offer or required submission to the Postmaster as a formal light duty request requiring PM approval.
### Complainant's Age-Based Theory

The Complainant argued that age was a factor in his removal from the facility, asserting that he was expected to complete an overburdened mail route and that, having grown older, he has noticed that his body does not recover from pain and injuries as quickly as it did during his youth.
He could not, however, provide specific examples of younger employees treated more favorably in similar circumstances.
## ADMINISTRATIVE ADJUDICATION

At the conclusion of the Agency's investigation, the Complainant received a copy of the Report of Investigation and written notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge.
The Complainant timely requested a hearing.

However, when he failed to lodge objections to the Agency's motion, the assigned Administrative Judge granted the Agency's December 14, 2023 motion for a decision rendered without an evidentiary hearing and issued a written decision on January 4, 2024.
The Administrative Judge found that the Complainant failed to establish that the Agency subjected him to discrimination and harassment as alleged.
The judge determined that the Agency's unrebutted factual findings established legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its personnel actions.

The Administrative Judge specifically noted that the Complainant had argued with supervisors, engaged in time-wasting activities while using his cellular telephone in the locker room, neglected to properly fasten his seatbelt, and failed to turn off his vehicle when exiting it.

The judge found that these established facts, which the Complainant did not dispute, provided substantial nondiscriminatory justification for the disciplinary measures and other management actions imposed.
The Administrative Judge concluded that the Complainant failed to present evidence demonstrating that management made age-based biased comments or treated younger workers more favorably.

Based on this analysis, the judge determined that no reasonable factfinder, even when viewing evidence in the light most favorable to the Complainant, could rationally conclude that the Agency's actions were motivated by age-related considerations.
The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully adopting and implementing the Administrative Judge's decision.
This action prompted the Complainant to file the instant appeal.

# CASE FILE RECORD - EEO COMPLAINT INVESTIGATION
**COMPLAINANT POSITION AND EMPLOYMENT:**

The complainant was employed as a PSE Sales and Services Distribution Associate, Grade Level 06 P, at the Agency's Cape Central Post Office in Cape Coral, Florida, during the relevant period of this investigation.
**FORMAL COMPLAINT FILING AND ALLEGATIONS:**
On April 4, 2022, the complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging racial harassment based on her race as a White employee.

She claimed that during February 2022, her first-line supervisor, an African American male, subjected her to racial slurs, made threatening statements regarding physical assault, and created a hostile work environment.
The complainant further alleged that when she reported these incidents to management officials, no corrective action was taken.
**DETAILED ALLEGATIONS:**
During the investigation, the complainant provided specific accounts of alleged incidents.
In late January or early February 2022, she reported that the supervisor told her not to clock out for lunch due to overtime.

# INVESTIGATION RECORD - CASE FILE DOCUMENT
## CASE BACKGROUND AND COMPLAINANT'S EMPLOYMENT STATUS

At the time of the events forming the basis of this complaint, the Complainant was employed as a Mail Processing Clerk at the Agency's Atlanta Processing and Distribution Center located in Atlanta, Georgia.

Prior to filing the current complaint, the Complainant had submitted an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint in September 2018, which remained pending before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) at the time the Complainant provided her affidavit for the instant complaint.
The Complainant's prior complaint involved allegations of sexual harassment by a co-worker, a matter that would subsequently prove relevant to her current claims.
## COMPLAINANT'S MEDICAL CONDITION AND DOCUMENTED RESTRICTIONS
The Complainant reported suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression resulting from an incident of sexual harassment and assault by a co-worker.
Beyond her mental health conditions, the Complainant also documented physical limitations affecting her ability to perform standard work duties.
Specifically, she suffers from back, foot, and knee issues that prevent her from standing or walking for extended periods.
Additionally, the Complainant has documented restrictions on climbing and descending stairs, as well as limitations on bending, stooping, and lifting activities.

Most significantly, the Complainant's physician provided written documentation stating that due to her PTSD resulting from the co-worker's sexual assault, she could no longer work in the same facility as the individual who assaulted her.
This medical restriction established a clear occupational need for relocation to accommodate her documented disability.
## TIMELINE OF EVENTS AND ALLEGED FAILURES TO ACCOMMODATE
The sexual harassment and assault incident occurred in September 2019.
Following this incident, the Complainant took Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) leave.
In April 2020, after her medical leave concluded, the Complainant was cleared to return to work at a facility different from her harasser.
However, upon her return, the Complainant discovered that her harasser remained at the original facility, apparently without any transfer or reassignment action having been taken.
In June 2020, the Complainant sustained a workplace knee injury.
She submitted documentation regarding this injury to the Agency in July 2020 but received no response.

When the Agency's Reasonable Accommodation Committee eventually requested additional documentation, the Committee ignored the Complainant's PTSD-related limitation requiring separation from her harasser and instead focused exclusively on her physical restrictions stemming from the knee injury.
The record reflects significant delays in addressing the Complainant's accommodation needs.

Not until July 2021—nearly two years after the initial sexual assault and approximately one year after her return-to-work clearance—was the Complainant finally provided a modified assignment at a different location that accommodated her physical restrictions.
Notably, the record contains no explanation or documentation concerning the nature of this new position or why the Agency required a full year to relocate the Complainant away from her harasser.
The Complainant went on COVID-related leave on August 16, 2021, and was subsequently hospitalized for sepsis.
She was not cleared to return to work until September 21, 2021.
However, from that date forward, the Complainant was not returned to work.
According to her account, management informed her only that no work was available based on her documented restrictions.

Critically, the record contains no statement from any Agency official documenting that any effort was undertaken to accommodate the Complainant's restrictions from September 2021 onward, nor any evidence that such accommodation efforts were attempted and failed.
## LEAVE AND BID POSITION DENIAL

The Complainant alleged that she should not have been placed on leave without pay (LWOP) beginning November 21, 2021, given that her inability to work resulted from the Agency's failure to accommodate her documented medical restrictions.
In January 2022, the Complainant submitted a bid for a position.
However, her bid was denied, and the position was awarded to another employee with less seniority.
The Complainant was marked "ineligible" with no explanation provided at the time of the denial.

When questioned about the bid denial, the Supervisor of Distribution Operations stated in her affidavit that the Complainant's bid was rejected because the Complainant had not provided updated medical documentation demonstrating that she could fully perform her duties within six months.
However, the record contains no evidence that the Complainant was ever formally requested to provide such documentation or informed that such documentation was required.
The Complainant consistently stated she received no explanation for the denial.

The Collective Bargaining Agreement governing this matter specifically provides that management may request medical certification at the time of bid submission or thereafter, but no evidence exists that the Complainant was informed of this procedural requirement.
## THE FORMAL EEO COMPLAINT

On May 13, 2022, the Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging discrimination by the Agency on the bases of race (African-American, Native American, and Cuban), sex (female), color (Brown), disability (both physical and mental), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity.
These allegations were made under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973.

The complaint specifically addressed three primary claims: failure to accommodate her medical restrictions since November 10, 2021; charging her LWOP since November 10, 2021; and denying her a bid position on January 24, 2022.

The Complainant also asserted three additional claims: denial of accommodation between April 2020 and November 9, 2021; improper coding of leave as workers' compensation (OWCP) leave on unspecified dates; and denial of insurance benefits on unspecified dates.
## AGENCY DISMISSALS AND PROCEDURAL DETERMINATIONS
The Agency issued a final decision on December 6, 2022, pursuant to applicable federal regulations.

The Agency found that the Complainant had not submitted required medical documentation to support reasonable accommodation requests or to demonstrate her ability to perform the bid position within six months.
The Agency also determined that the Complainant had not established pretext for discrimination.
Regarding the additional claims, the Agency dismissed the denial of reasonable accommodation claim for dates prior to November 10, 2021, citing untimely EEO counselor contact.
The Agency further dismissed the leave coding and insurance benefits claims as collateral attacks on the workers' compensation adjudicatory process.
The Complainant subsequently appealed this decision.

# INVESTIGATION RECORD – CASE FILE DOCUMENTATION
## COMPLAINANT BACKGROUND AND INITIAL COMPLAINT
The complainant was employed by the Agency as a Taxpayer Advocate at the Laguna Niguel, California office during the period under review.

On November 4, 2021, the complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint asserting that the Agency had discriminated against her on the basis of race (Hispanic) and national origin (Mexican).
The Agency formally accepted this complaint for investigation by letter dated November 16, 2021.
## ALLEGATIONS AND FRAMING OF CLAIMS

The Agency framed the formal complaint as an investigation into whether a co-worker serving as an On-the-Job Instructor (OJI) and Lead subjected the complainant to harassment based on her race and national origin.
The alleged harassment reportedly occurred on multiple occasions beginning in June 2020 and continuing through July 2021.
The specific allegations included four categories of conduct:
First, the OJI/Lead made derogatory comments about the complainant's accent and stated a dislike for communicating with her.

Second, the OJI/Lead allegedly attempted to sabotage the complainant's work by creating lists of inventory issues and expired casework, while providing intentionally false guidance regarding case processing procedures.
Third, the OJI/Lead filled the complainant's calendar with unrealistic appointment schedules that would have been difficult for even experienced employees to complete.
Fourth, the OJI/Lead advised the complainant's manager to have her process a fraudulent tax return.
## INVESTIGATION PROCESS AND AGENCY DECISION

Following completion of the investigation, the Agency provided the complainant with a copy of the investigative report and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge, as provided in 29 C.F.R.
The complainant did not timely request such a hearing.
Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b), concluding that no discrimination had occurred.

The Agency's final decision acknowledged that if the initial supervisor (S1) had indeed made the comments described in the first allegation regarding the complainant's accent, such statements would constitute unwelcome verbal conduct based on the complainant's protected categories.

However, regarding the remaining allegations, the Agency determined that the complainant had failed to produce persuasive evidence that management's actions were harassment based on statutorily protected classes.
The Agency noted that the complainant's uncorroborated assertions that race, ethnicity, and national origin motivated management's conduct were insufficient to meet her burden of proof.
The Agency also referenced an internal anti-harassment inquiry that did not substantiate the complainant's claims.
## COMPLAINANT'S APPEAL ARGUMENTS

On appeal, the complainant asserted that the Agency's final decision failed to adequately recognize that the alleged harasser was initially her former manager before later serving as her Lead and OJI.
The complainant reiterated that S1 made derogatory comments regarding her accent beginning on her first day of employment.

She further asserted that she had notified another supervisor (S2) of S1's harassing behavior and requested a supervisory change, but that S2 failed to address the harassment and permitted the conduct to continue.
## AGENCY'S RESPONSE
The Agency requested affirmation of its final decision.

Regarding the accent-related comments, the Agency argued that even accepting the complainant's allegations as true, S1's comments did not indicate mockery based on Mexican descent but rather reflected difficulty in communication.
The Agency characterized such comments as insensitive remarks that the Commission has traditionally declined to find discriminatory.
The Agency asserted that the complainant failed to establish the severity and pervasiveness required for a hostile work environment finding.
Additionally, the Agency noted that management promptly separated the complainant and S1 after the harassment was raised in late July 2021, with no subsequent contact occurring between them.

# OFFICIAL CASE FILE DOCUMENT
## Investigation Record and Administrative Decision Summary
BACKGROUND AND EMPLOYMENT CONTEXT

This case involves a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint filed by a Counseling Psychologist and Licensed Marriage and Family Therapist who was employed at the Agency's Health Clinic located in Baumholder, Germany.

At the time the events giving rise to this complaint occurred, the Complainant held a professional clinical position responsible for providing mental health services, including marriage and family counseling, to the clinic's patient population.

The period covered by this investigation spans from September 2014 through January 2017, representing a significant period during which the Complainant experienced various workplace challenges and filed multiple formal complaints with different Agency offices and oversight bodies, including an Administrative Grievance filed in November 2014 and subsequent complaints to the Regional Health Command-Europe Inspector General (IG) office in October 2016.
## II.
ALLEGATIONS AND COMPLAINTS
General Workplace Environment Concerns (September 2014 - Present)
The Complainant alleged that beginning in September 2014 and continuing throughout her employment, management failed to provide her with necessary professional development and training opportunities.
She asserted that she was subjected to what she characterized as demeaning treatment, including derogatory comments, unjustified interrogations, and excessive criticism of her work performance.
The Complainant further claimed to experience non-verbal forms of hostility, including negative facial expressions from supervisory and managerial personnel.
Additionally, the Complainant alleged that her professional authority was systematically undermined through various mechanisms.

She contended that coworkers and other employees were encouraged to bypass the established chain of command, and that her clinical decisions regarding patient care were frequently overruled without appropriate justification.
According to her account, these actions made it impossible for her to effectively execute the duties and responsibilities of her position as a clinical mental health professional.

The Complainant further alleged that she was required to expend considerable energy defending herself against what she characterized as false portrayals and claims made by supervisors and other employees.
She asserted that Agency officials used their positions of authority to disparage her professional reputation and to isolate her within the workplace.
She claimed that despite her work efforts, her contributions were neither recognized nor appropriately rewarded.

The Complainant reported these concerns through her supervisory chain on multiple occasions, yet alleged that the Agency failed to conduct thorough investigations or to address and remediate the underlying causes of her concerns.
Client Assignment and Scheduling Issues
The Complainant alleged that on unspecified dates, other employees unilaterally rescheduled her clients with alternative providers without her knowledge or consent.
As a result of these actions, when patients requested to continue their therapeutic relationship with the Complainant, they were informed that such arrangements were not permitted.
This action effectively removed the Complainant's caseload and professional responsibilities without formal clinical review or documented clinical justification.
October 5, 2016 Staff Meeting Incident

During a staff meeting held on October 5, 2016, the Complainant alleged that a Captain made clinical decisions regarding her patients without soliciting or considering her input, despite her being the primary treating clinician for these patients.
The Complainant viewed this action as a failure to respect her professional clinical judgment and authority.
October 12, 2016 Meeting with Command Staff

On October 12, 2016, the Complainant met with the Lieutenant Colonel (identified as Deputy Chief of Clinical Services and Chief Nursing Officer) and the Lieutenant (identified as Commander of Baumholder and Kaiserslautern Clinics) to discuss her request for reassignment from the Baumholder Team.
During this meeting, the Complainant alleged that she felt personally attacked, primarily through what she perceived as disrespectful tone of voice and aggressive demeanor from both officials.
November 12, 2016 Performance Evaluation
The Complainant challenged the accuracy and truthfulness of a performance evaluation issued on or about November 12, 2016.
She asserted that the evaluation failed to fairly and accurately characterize her work performance based on her understanding of her actual job performance.
December 21, 2016 Caseload Reduction

Upon returning to work on December 21, 2016, following a two-day sick leave absence (December 19-20, 2016), the Complainant discovered that two clients had been removed from her schedule and reassigned to other providers.

The Complainant further alleged that despite an acknowledged shortage of behavioral health providers within the office due to holiday staffing shortages, staff members refused to engage her to assist in covering cases or addressing the documented provider shortage.
Staff Integration Issues

The Complainant alleged that the Non-Commissioned Officer-In-Charge (NCOIC) brought a new staff member to the clinic and proceeded to introduce this individual to all providers and other staff members within the office.
However, despite the fact that the NCOIC was conversing with the Complainant directly outside her office at the time, the new staff member was not introduced to the Complainant.
The Complainant claimed not to know the identity of this new staff member as a result of this alleged slight.
Investigation and Legal Representation Issues
In October 2016, the Complainant contacted the Regional Health Command-Europe Inspector General regarding allegations of discrimination and harassment.
On December 6, 2016, the Sergeant First Class, representing the IG office, contacted the Complainant to discuss her complaint.
The Complainant indicated that her legal counsel would be in Germany during the week of January 9, 2017, and she desired to coordinate a meeting with the IG office.
Her counsel subsequently emailed the Sergeant First Class seeking clarification regarding the purpose and nature of the proposed meeting.
However, the Sergeant First Class did not respond to this communication, and the anticipated meeting did not occur.
Developmental Counseling and Reassignment

On January 27, 2017, the Complainant received developmental counseling regarding a temporary reassignment that had been implemented on January 4, 2017, to the Landstuhl Regional Medical Center (LRMC).
## III.
PRIOR ADMINISTRATIVE ACTION
The Complainant's initial concerns regarding workplace conditions were previously addressed through the Agency's Administrative Grievance process.
On November 28, 2014, the Complainant filed a formal Administrative Grievance that included many of the claims subsequently included in the present EEO complaint.

In response to this grievance, on January 30, 2015, the Complainant received a notice of decision stating that she had been granted her requested remedy, which consisted of formal mediation to work through her concerns and improve the work environment.
The Administrative Grievance was closed following this resolution.
## IV.
INVESTIGATION FINDINGS AND AGENCY RESPONSES
Training and Professional Development

Regarding the Complainant's allegations concerning denial of training opportunities, the Commander of the Baumholder, Landstuhl, and Kaiserslautern Clinics stated that the Complainant had expressed her desire to participate in a non-military professional development session regarding suicide and military personnel.

The Commander indicated that while the Agency could not fund her participation in what he characterized as personal research, he offered to provide her the time necessary to participate, though without financial support.

In a separate request, the Lieutenant stated that while he had approved the Complainant's request to attend a Suicide Prevention training scheduled in Vicenza, Italy, no funds were available for attendance.
The Lieutenant further noted that the training was ultimately cancelled, rendering the funding issue moot.
Client Transfer Incidents and September 20, 2016 Email

On September 20, 2016, the Complainant sent an email to the Supervisory Psychologist and Chief of Behavioral Health alleging that a Nurse Practitioner had informed two of her patients that they were being transferred to another provider for treatment, and had informed another patient that the Complainant was no longer working at the clinic and could not see him.

During the investigation, the Social Services Assistant noted that the Complainant had previously stated that she worked exclusively with marriage and family counseling patients, which limitation had led to some patient transfers and restricted the patient population she could serve.
The Nurse Practitioner similarly confirmed this restriction in her professional scope of practice.
The Lieutenant Colonel reported that he had investigated the client transfer situation and resolved the matter.
In one instance, he determined that a transfer had been unintentional, and the client was reassigned back to the Complainant's care.
October 5, 2016 High-Risk Meeting and ICE Complaints

On October 5 and 7, 2016, two separate Interactive Customer Evaluation (ICE) complaints were submitted by two different patients of the Complainant's regarding her standard of care to the Inspector General office.
On October 5, 2016, during a standard High-Risk meeting, a Captain discussed clinical concerns regarding two of the Complainant's patients.
Immediately following this meeting, the Complainant spoke with the Captain.

The Captain asserted that the Complainant had been aggressive during their conversation, had recorded the discussion without her consent, and had spoken loudly about the two patients in an open space within earshot of other patients.
The Captain denied making any changes to patient care decisions as a result of the discussion.
The Captain characterized the October 5 meeting as a standard coordination of care discussion that routinely occurred with all providers.

The Social Services Assistant confirmed that High-Risk meetings were conducted to enable various providers to coordinate appropriate patient care, and that all providers were expected to contribute their clinical perspectives.
She further stated that no provider was being told how to conduct their clinical work.

Following this meeting, the Complainant spoke with the Lieutenant Colonel, expressing that she no longer wished to participate in High-Risk meetings and requesting reassignment from the Baumholder Team.

During the October 12, 2016 meeting with the Lieutenant Colonel and Lieutenant to discuss the Complainant's request for removal from the Baumholder Team, both officials noted that while the Complainant repeatedly alleged that the work environment was hostile, she was unable to provide specific examples or detailed instances when pressed for such information.
During this meeting, the Complainant asserted that both the Lieutenant Colonel and another Colonel had been hostile toward her.

Inspector General Investigation and Report
The IG issued its formal report on November 15, 2016, based on the complaints submitted on October 5, 7, and 13, 2016.
The IG investigation concluded that there was insufficient evidence to support the Complainant's allegations of harassment or discrimination by Agency personnel.
However, the IG report did identify that the Complainant had created a disruptive work environment within the Baumholder Behavioral Health Clinic.
The report noted that the Complainant's interactions with other behavioral health staff members were contentious in nature.

The primary recommendation issued by the IG was to reassign the Complainant out of the Baumholder Health Clinic, citing concerns that her continued assignment to the clinic would result in ongoing conflict with other team members, which demonstrably impacted patient care and significantly decreased morale throughout the clinical unit.
Notably, the IG report also found that the Complainant had violated German law by unlawfully recording a conversation without the other party's consent on November 15, 2016.

The Lieutenant Colonel issued a performance evaluation to the Complainant on or about November 12, 2016, based on fifteen standard performance metrics.
The Lieutenant Colonel documented that the Complainant received eleven "Exceed" ratings and four "Met" ratings across these metrics.
The areas marked as "Met" specifically related to collaboration with staff.
The Lieutenant Colonel provided detailed examples to support his ratings, noting that for the period from May 2016 through October 31, 2016, there was minimal collaboration with staff.
Despite the four "Met" ratings, the Complainant ultimately received an overall "Excellent" rating on the performance evaluation.

ADMINISTRATIVE HEARING AND FINAL DECISION

Following the completion of the EEO investigation, the Complainant was provided with a copy of the investigation report and was notified of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ).
The Complainant timely requested such a hearing.

On October 18, 2021, the Agency submitted a Motion for a Decision Without a Hearing, contending that the investigative record was sufficiently developed to permit resolution of the matter without further proceedings.
The Complainant submitted a response to this motion.
On January 31, 2022, the Administrative Judge issued his formal decision.
The AJ determined that the investigative record was adequately developed and contained sufficient evidence to permit a decision on the merits.

After making all reasonable inferences in favor of the Complainant, as required by EEO regulations, the AJ concluded that there were no material facts in dispute that would preclude summary disposition.

Regarding the substantive merits of the Complainant's discrimination claim, the AJ determined that the Agency had articulated legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for each of the employment actions challenged by the Complainant.

The AJ further determined that the Complainant had failed to present sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Agency's stated reasons were pretextual or were merely a cover for unlawful discriminatory motivation.

The AJ characterized the Complainant's complaint as primarily reflecting her dissatisfaction with her coworkers and management, as well as her expression of personal grievances, rather than demonstrating unlawful workplace conduct.
The Administrative Judge granted the Agency's Motion for a Decision Without a Hearing.
When the Agency failed to issue a final administrative action, the Administrative Judge's decision became the Agency's final administrative action by operation of law, in accordance with 29 C.F.R.

# INVESTIGATION RECORD - CASE FILE DOCUMENTATION
## CASE BACKGROUND AND PARTIES
This investigation record documents formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaints filed by two individuals (hereinafter "Complainants") against a federal agency (hereinafter "Agency").

At the time of the events giving rise to the complaints, both Complainants were employed as Emergency Management Specialists in the positions of Regional and National Tribal Government Liaisons at the Agency's First Responder Network Authority.
Complainants performed their duties remotely from locations in California, with one working from Pauma Valley and the other from Thousand Palms.
Both individuals commenced employment with the Agency in October 2015, initially hired at the Pay Band IV level.
## FORMAL COMPLAINTS AND PROTECTED GROUNDS
On June 13, 2019, each Complainant independently filed comprehensive formal EEO complaints alleging unlawful discrimination, harassment, and retaliatory actions by the Agency.
The complaints identified three protected bases for discrimination: race (specifically, Native American status), national origin (Native American ancestry), and sex.
Additionally, Complainants alleged that they experienced reprisal for engaging in prior protected EEO activity.

It should be noted that Complainants subsequently withdrew their claims of sex discrimination during the formal hearing process, narrowing the focus of their allegations to the remaining protected bases.
## SUBSTANTIVE ALLEGATIONS - DISCRIMINATORY PAY AND COMPENSATION
The primary allegation centers on systematic discrimination in pay and compensation.
Complainants assert that since their initial hiring, they have been subjected to disparate treatment regarding salary negotiations and pay band assignments.

Complainant 1 specifically alleges that during pre-employment negotiations, Agency representatives informed him that the Agency would only offer him 70 percent of his previous wages and stated that he could "accept this offer or decline it entirely." Complainant 1 further contends that non-Native employees did not encounter similar constraints during their hiring negotiations.

Complainant 2 claims that the Agency failed to properly account for her prior salary history and teaching wages in calculating her initial offer, instead providing compensation based solely on her current tribal salary.

Both Complainants assert that they performed substantially identical work to peers who were hired at the Pay Band V level, yet they themselves were hired at the lower Pay Band IV level and received compensation at the lowest tier available.

This disparity in pay classification created a cascading barrier to career advancement, as Complainants later discovered that senior leadership positions were available exclusively to employees at the Pay Band V level.
## MANAGEMENT RESPONSE TO PAY DISPARITIES

In April 2018, the Executive Director of the Public Safety Advocacy Directorate directed Complainants' supervisor ("Supervisor 1") to conduct a comprehensive review addressing wage and pay band disparities within the organization.

However, after the review was completed, both the Executive Director and a Senior Director took no corrective action and failed to acknowledge that such a review had ever been commissioned or completed.
During a telephone conversation on May 31, 2018, the Senior Director claimed to have no knowledge of the April 2018 review.
Subsequently, Complainants learned from Supervisor 1 that the Senior Director was, in fact, fully aware of the review and its contents.

In January 2019, the Executive Director acknowledged to Supervisor 2 (Complainants' subsequent supervisor) that he had received the completed review but stated that he felt no institutional obligation to act upon its findings or recommendations.
## PERSONNEL POLICIES AND PROCEDURAL FAILURES
On June 15, 2018, Complainants inquired with the Deputy Chief Administrative Officer regarding hiring authorities and direct hiring procedures available within the Agency.

They were informed that the Agency "does not have established personnel policies and practices." The Deputy Chief Administrative Officer and Chief Administrative Officer further failed to advise Complainants of their rights to pursue formal EEO processes to address and remediate their allegations of discriminatory compensation.
## ORGANIZATIONAL RESTRUCTURING AND HARASSMENT ALLEGATIONS
In June 2018, Complainants underwent a reorganization process that they characterize as deliberately designed to "bury" them more deeply within the organizational hierarchy.

Complainants allege that this restructuring was undertaken in an effort to provoke them to voluntarily resign from their positions and, additionally, served as a mechanism to "limit any escalation of human resources issues originating from the tribal team."
## DISCRIMINATORY WORKING CONDITIONS AND RESOURCE DENIAL

Since June 2018 on an ongoing basis, Complainants have been required to develop and maintain separate strategic plans, while none of their non-Tribal team peers have been subjected to similar requirements.
Additionally, Complainants were precluded from accessing resources on an equal basis with their counterparts.
They were required to coordinate all activities through a separate, discriminatory process to access resources and tribal shareholders.
This included being compelled to engage with contracting staff and tribal shareholders exclusively through a designated "gatekeeper" and being prohibited from participating in certain meetings.
An Agency Contracting Officer's Representative was mandated to attend all daily engagements between contractors and Complainants.
## HOSTILE CONTRACTOR TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT INACTION

Between June 2018 and February 2019, Complainants and other Agency officials repeatedly notified senior leadership that tribal team members were experiencing hostile and discriminatory treatment from officials employed by an Agency contractor.
Despite these persistent complaints, senior leadership neither remedied the situation nor took disciplinary action against the contractor.
Instead, senior leadership allegedly condoned the contractor's conduct and continued to place Complainants in hostile working environments with these contractor officials.
## PUBLIC RECOGNITION FAILURE
On May 5, 2019, the Agency issued a public social media communication thanking local, state, and federal workers for their service and dedication.
Notably, this communication failed to acknowledge or reference Complainants and other tribal team members, despite their contributions to the Agency's mission.
## ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING AND APPEALS
Following investigation, Complainants received copies of investigative files and requested hearings before EEOC Administrative Judges.
The complaints were assigned to different Administrative Judges in the Commission's Washington Field Office.
Both Complainants' shared legal counsel filed consolidation motions, which the Agency opposed.
One Administrative Judge denied consolidation while the other did not address the motion.
Both Administrative Judges issued separate summary judgment decisions concluding that no discrimination or unlawful retaliation had been established.
The Agency subsequently implemented these decisions as final actions.
Both Complainants have filed appeals from these determinations.

## COMPLAINANT EMPLOYMENT AND SUPERVISORY RELATIONSHIP

At the time of the events giving rise to this formal complaint, the Complainant was employed as a Registered Nurse assigned to the 4 East Medical-Surgical Unit at the Veterans Affairs Medical Center (VAMC) located in West Los Angeles, California.

During the relevant period covered by this investigation, the Complainant's immediate supervisor and first-line manager was the Nurse Manager for the 4 East Medical-Surgical Unit, hereinafter referred to as "S1" in this investigative record.
## SUMMARY OF ALLEGATIONS
The Complainant raised fourteen distinct allegations against her employer and supervisor, which are detailed below.

The Agency's Office of Resolution Management (ORM) initially issued a Notice of Partial Acceptance, which dismissed a portion of Claim 7 for failure to state a claim, while accepting the remaining allegations for investigation.
The Agency ultimately accepted thirteen claims for formal investigation and analysis.
### Claim 1: Scheduling Dispute and Shift Modification Demand
The Complainant alleged that S1 demanded that she work twelve-hour shifts, which the Complainant refused to do.
During the investigation, it was discovered that the original claim description was inaccurate.
The Complainant later clarified in a supplemental affidavit that the event did not occur in May 2018 as initially stated, but rather took place in November or December 2017.

The Complainant further clarified that she had not requested to work twelve-hour shifts; rather, S1 had allegedly demanded that the Complainant change her work schedule from eight-hour shifts to twelve-hour shifts.
The ORM noted that Claim 1 constituted a timely raised independently actionable claim and was also incorporated into the broader harassment allegations.
### Claim 2: Unauthorized Disclosure of Confidential Medical Information
In May 2018, the Complainant alleged that S1 disclosed the Complainant's confidential medical information in violation of the Rehabilitation Act.
Specifically, the Complainant claimed that S1, speaking loudly within earshot of coworkers, stated: "And you, you need to go somewhere else to have your surgery.

If the VA is not taking care of you, you need to go to UCLA." This statement allegedly occurred as S1 was walking down the hallway between the reception station and the nurses' station, following the Complainant's presentation of leave documentation in S1's private office.
The Complainant identified two witnesses to this incident.
Witness 1 allegedly heard S1 discussing the Complainant's surgery and asked if the Complainant was okay.
Witness 13 reportedly observed S1 speaking loudly from the reception station and questioned why S1 was telling everyone about the Complainant's surgery.
The Complainant contended that this public disclosure violated her rights under the Rehabilitation Act.
### Claim 3: Improper Access to Confidential Medical Records
During January 2019, the Complainant alleged that she was required to work with coworkers who had improperly and without authorization accessed her confidential medical records.

Upon receiving the report, the Complainant reviewed the documentation and identified six coworkers whom she believed had accessed her medical records improperly.
The report provided included four columns: employee names, dates and times of access, specific notes regarding the type of access (such as "CPRS Chart version 1, Appointment Management, Case No.

Exam Edit, Register Patient, Clinical Scheduling"), and designations indicating "Yes" or "No." The Complainant marked six names with arrows and added handwritten notes indicating where each employee worked.

Subsequently, on June 18, 2019, the Complainant submitted an email to the Privacy Office identifying three specific nurses—Coworker 2, Coworker 3, and Coworker 4—as having inappropriately accessed her medical record.
The Privacy Office investigation determined that Coworker 4 accessed the Complainant's medical records on June 15, 2018, and had no valid clinical reason for doing so.
Coworker 4 subsequently stated that "everyone was talking about [Complainant's] surgery" and that she had witnessed another employee accessing the Complainant's medical record.
The investigation further found that Coworker 3 had accessed the Complainant's medical records six times throughout 2018 and 2019.
Coworker 3 stated she accessed the records because the Complainant had written her up on several occasions and she did not want to work on the same shift as the Complainant.
The Privacy Investigation Report concluded that Coworker 3 accessed this information intentionally, despite it having no relevance to scheduling purposes or job-related duties.

On July 1, 2019, the Privacy Officer issued a letter to the Complainant confirming that two coworkers—identified only as Coworker 4 and one additional employee—had inappropriately accessed her medical record outside the scope of their duties and responsibilities.
The letter noted that the other employees identified by the Complainant had accessed her records within their job responsibilities.
Supervisory staff of the identified employees were notified, and both employees were recommended to immediately retake mandatory privacy and security training.

### Claim 7: Accusations of Intimidating, Aggressive, and Harassing Conduct

On May 1, 2019, the Complainant was accused by a coworker—who the Complainant contended was actually bullying and harassing her—of being intimidating and aggressive and of engaging in harassing behavior.
The Agency's ORM partially dismissed this claim for failure to state a claim but accepted the remaining portion as part of the overall harassment allegation.
### Claim 8: Accusation of Unauthorized Email Access
On May 3, 2019, the Complainant was accused of sending an email from another employee's email account.
This allegation was investigated as part of the broader disciplinary actions taken against the Complainant.
### Claim 9: Demand to Sign Misconduct Form
On May 3, 2019, S1 requested that the Complainant sign a misconduct form in connection with the allegations raised in Claim 8.

Also on May 28, 2019, S1 accused the Complainant of engaging in misconduct.
This accusation was made contemporaneously with S1's alleged pacing behavior described in Claim 10.
### Claim 12: Interference with Privacy Violation Investigation
On June 6, 2019, the Complainant alleged that an unnamed employee interfered with the Complainant's privacy violation investigation.
The Complainant did not provide specific details regarding the nature of this alleged interference.

On August 20, 2019, the Complainant discovered an article posted on the report table regarding nurses with mental disabilities.
The Complainant believed this article had been directed at her personally, thereby constituting harassment based on her disability status.
### Claim 14: Pattern of Supervisory Mismanagement
On unspecified dates, the Complainant alleged that S1 "split the staff against each other" and failed to properly resolve issues that occurred on the unit floor.
This allegation was characterized as part of a broader pattern of hostile work environment conduct.
## INVESTIGATIVE FINDINGS
### Analysis of Claim 1: Scheduling Dispute
The Agency's investigation established through undisputed evidence that the Complainant remained on her eight-hour tour of duty at all times.
The Agency therefore found that Claim 1 was not supported by the record.
Furthermore, even accepting the Complainant's allegation as true, the Agency found no indication of discriminatory motive behind any alleged demand to change her work schedule.
### Analysis of Claim 2: Unauthorized Medical Information Disclosure
Regarding the alleged public disclosure of the Complainant's surgical needs, S1 asserted that she had discussed the Complainant's surgery only in private to offer emotional support.
S1 further argued that there was no evidence beyond the Complainant's subjective testimony that anyone actually overheard the statement made in the hallway.
The investigative record indicates that six coworkers were interviewed as part of the privacy investigation process.
All six coworkers confirmed that S1 had not disclosed any information about the Complainant's surgery or any other confidential medical information to them.
Instead, these coworkers stated they learned of the Complainant's surgery because the Complainant herself shared this information directly with them.
The investigative record further documents that the Complainant acknowledged telling at least one coworker that she was going to have surgery, though it had been canceled.
The Agency concluded that the Complainant failed to demonstrate that S1 improperly disclosed her confidential medical information.

The Agency further noted that even if it were to credit the Complainant's version of the incident and assume that others overheard the statement—which the Agency found no evidence to support—the vague reference allegedly made by S1 would not constitute a disclosure of confidential medical information.
### Analysis of Claim 3: Improper Medical Record Access

The Agency noted that, pursuant to established Equal Employment Opportunity Commission precedent, allegations that the Privacy Act has been violated are not within the purview of EEOC regulations absent a further allegation that the Privacy Act violation resulted from prohibited discrimination.
The Agency determined that the Complainant failed to provide evidence of discriminatory animus based on her disability.

The privacy investigation established that the two coworkers who accessed the Complainant's medical records did so to determine when the Complainant would be out for surgery and, in one instance, because the coworker did not want to work during the same shifts as the Complainant.
The Agency found no indication and no evidence of discriminatory motivation or wrongdoing beyond the Privacy Act violation itself.
Although the investigation confirmed that privacy violations had occurred, the Agency concluded that these violations were not motivated by prohibited discrimination related to disability status.
### Analysis of Claim 12: Alleged Interference with Investigation

Regarding the alleged interference with the privacy violation investigation, the Agency stated there was no indication of any alleged "resistance" from the Complainant's coworkers during the Privacy Investigation process.
The Agency noted that even if such resistance were accepted as true, there was no evidence that any such resistance was based on discriminatory animus.
The Agency emphasized that S1 had promptly reported the Complainant's concern regarding privacy violations to the Privacy Office.
A comprehensive privacy investigation was subsequently conducted, and all employees identified by the Complainant as potentially accessing her medical records were interviewed.
Two employees were identified as having improperly accessed the Complainant's records, and both were subsequently disciplined and ordered to retake privacy training.
The Agency found no evidence that any failure to take additional or more severe disciplinary measures was motivated by discriminatory animus.
### Analysis of Hostile Work Environment Claim
The Agency conducted a comprehensive analysis of all harassment allegations raised by the Complainant.
Even accepting all of the Complainant's allegations as true, the Agency concluded that she had presented no evidence that she was singled out for treatment based on her disability status.

The Agency noted that Witness 1, who had not been employed by the VAMC since 2018, provided only a vague statement alleging that S1 had told him the Complainant was having "mental issues." This statement was directly contradicted by S1's testimony.
S1 indicated that she was unaware the Complainant had a disability.
S1 noted that although she was aware the Complainant had taken bereavement leave following the death of a parent, to S1's knowledge, this leave was not related to any mental or other disability.
Witness 2's statement gave no indication that S1 harbored discriminatory animus against the Complainant based on disability status.
The Agency noted that both witnesses expressed personal complaints about S1, rendering their statements less credible in the investigative context.
The Agency concluded that the Complainant failed to establish that she had been subjected to unlawful harassment based on her disability or other protected status.
## ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURES

Following the completion of the investigation, the Agency provided the Complainant with a copy of the full Report of Investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ).
The Complainant initially requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew that request.
Consequently, the Agency issued a Final Decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b), adopting the investigative findings and providing the Complainant with the agency's formal determination on each claim.
**END OF INVESTIGATION RECORD**

# INVESTIGATION RECORD - CASE FILE DOCUMENTATION
## BACKGROUND AND COMPLAINANTS' EMPLOYMENT STATUS
The complainants in this matter were employed by the Agency as Emergency Management Specialists with responsibilities as Regional and National Tribal Government Liaisons.

At the time the events giving rise to these complaints occurred, both complainants were performing their duties remotely—one from Pauma Valley, California, and the other from Thousand Palms, California.
The complainants initiated their employment relationship with the Agency in October 2015, beginning at the Pay Band IV compensation level.

On June 13, 2019, both complainants filed formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaints with the Agency, alleging discrimination and harassment based on their race (Native American), national origin (Native American), and in retaliation for prior protected EEO activity.
Additionally, complainants initially alleged discrimination based on sex; however, this claim was subsequently withdrawn during the hearing process.
## ALLEGED DISCRIMINATORY COMPENSATION PRACTICES
### Initial Hiring and Salary Negotiations
The complainants alleged systematic discrimination in compensation dating from their initial hire.

Specifically, Complainant 1 reported that during pre-employment salary negotiations, he was informed by the Agency that it was obligated only to offer him seventy percent of his previous wage, with the explicit statement that he could "take it or leave it." Complainant 1 further contended that non-Native employees were not subjected to comparable treatment during their respective hiring processes.

Complainant 2 alleged that the Agency failed to properly account for changes in her prior salary history or her teaching background, instead offering only compensation commensurate with her then-current tribal salary.
### Disparate Pay Bands and Job Classification

Both complainants asserted that they performed substantially identical work as peer employees who were hired at the Pay Band V level, yet they themselves were hired at Pay Band IV and maintained at the lowest compensation tier.
This disparity in classification, the complainants argued, directly resulted from discriminatory intent based on their Native American status.
### Failure to Address Documented Pay Disparities
The complainants documented what they characterized as management's deliberate inaction regarding known compensation inequities.

In approximately April 2018, the Executive Director of the Public Safety Advocacy Directorate directed Complainants' supervisor to conduct a comprehensive review addressing wage and pay band disparities within the department.

However, subsequent to the completion of this review, the Executive Director and a Senior Director allegedly took no remedial action and failed to acknowledge that such a review had even been commissioned.
This pattern of non-responsiveness continued when, during a May 31, 2018 telephone conversation, the Senior Director claimed to have no knowledge of the April 2018 review.
The complainants later learned from their supervisor that the Senior Director was, in fact, "very well aware" of the review's existence and findings.

When complainants inquired on June 15, 2018, with the Deputy Chief Administrative Officer regarding hiring authorities and direct hiring procedures, they were informed that the Agency "does not have personnel policies and practices." This same official also failed to advise the complainants of their rights to pursue the EEO process to address their allegations of discriminatory compensation.
By July 2018, when Complainants' new supervisor inquired about the April 2018 review, the Executive Director and Senior Director denied any knowledge of having committed to such an investigation.
Most significantly, in January 2019, the Executive Director acknowledged to Supervisor 2 that he had indeed received the review but asserted that he felt no obligation to act upon its findings.

The Executive Director then instructed the supervisor to "tamper any escalation of HR issues for the tribal team." In a subsequent email, the Executive Director attempted to retreat from these instructions, claiming that the supervisor had misunderstood his directive.
## CAREER ADVANCEMENT RESTRICTIONS AND ORGANIZATIONAL CHANGES

The complainants alleged that the discriminatory establishment of their compensation at the Pay Band IV level effectively precluded them from applying to senior leadership positions, as the Agency made such positions available exclusively to Pay Band V employees.
This created a structural barrier to advancement based on the initial discriminatory classification.

Additionally, complainants contended that in June 2018, they were "buried deeper" within the organizational structure through a reorganization process undertaken with the express intent of provoking them to resign and as a mechanism to "limit any HR escalations from the tribal team."
## DIFFERENTIAL TREATMENT IN WORK ASSIGNMENTS AND RESOURCES
From June 2018 onward, complainants were required to create separate strategic plans on an ongoing basis, while their non-Tribal team peers were not subjected to this requirement.
Furthermore, complainants alleged that they were systematically denied equal access to resources necessary to perform their duties in the same manner as their non-Tribal counterparts.
Access to resources and non-federal shareholders was forced through a separate, discriminatory process.

Complainants were required to engage with contracting staff and Tribal shareholders through an intermediary "gatekeeper." The Agency further restricted the categories of meetings in which complainants were permitted to participate and required that an Agency Contracting Officer's Representative be present during all daily engagements between contractors and complainants.
## HOSTILE WORK ENVIRONMENT AND CONTRACTOR CONDUCT

Between June 2018 and February 2019, complainants and other Agency officials repeatedly informed senior leadership that Tribal team members were subjected to hostile and discriminatory treatment by representatives of an Agency contractor.

Despite these repeated notifications, senior leadership condoned the contractors' conduct and continued to place the Tribal team in situations involving hostile interactions with contracting officials.
## PUBLIC RECOGNITION OMISSION
On May 5, 2019, the Agency issued a public statement via social media thanking local, state, and federal workers for their dedication and service in connection with their work.
However, the Agency failed to acknowledge or reference the Tribal team members, despite their substantial contributions to the same initiatives.
## ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS
Following the completion of investigations, the complainants received copies of their investigative files and requested hearings before EEOC Administrative Judges.
The complaints were assigned to different Administrative Judges within the Commission's Washington Field Office.
Complainants' legal representative filed motions to consolidate the complaints for joint processing before each judge.
The Agency opposed these consolidation motions.
One Administrative Judge denied the consolidation motion while the other judge did not issue a ruling on the motion.
Both judges subsequently issued separate summary judgment decisions concluding that no discrimination or unlawful retaliation had been established.
The Agency implemented the Administrative Judges' decisions as its final action.
Both complainants subsequently filed appeals challenging these determinations.

Most significantly, in January 2019, the Executive Director acknowledged to Supervisor 2 that he had indeed received the review but asserted that he felt no obligation to act upon its findings.

The Executive Director then instructed the supervisor to "tamper any escalation of HR issues for the tribal team." In a subsequent email, the Executive Director attempted to retreat from these instructions, claiming that the supervisor had misunderstood his directive.
