The complainants alleged that the discriminatory establishment of their compensation at the Pay Band IV level effectively precluded them from applying to senior leadership positions, as the Agency made such positions available exclusively to Pay Band V employees.
This created a structural barrier to advancement based on the initial discriminatory classification.

Additionally, complainants contended that in June 2018, they were "buried deeper" within the organizational structure through a reorganization process undertaken with the express intent of provoking them to resign and as a mechanism to "limit any HR escalations from the tribal team."
## DIFFERENTIAL TREATMENT IN WORK ASSIGNMENTS AND RESOURCES
From June 2018 onward, complainants were required to create separate strategic plans on an ongoing basis, while their non-Tribal team peers were not subjected to this requirement.
Furthermore, complainants alleged that they were systematically denied equal access to resources necessary to perform their duties in the same manner as their non-Tribal counterparts.
Access to resources and non-federal shareholders was forced through a separate, discriminatory process.

Complainants were required to engage with contracting staff and Tribal shareholders through an intermediary "gatekeeper." The Agency further restricted the categories of meetings in which complainants were permitted to participate and required that an Agency Contracting Officer's Representative be present during all daily engagements between contractors and complainants.
## HOSTILE WORK ENVIRONMENT AND CONTRACTOR CONDUCT

Between June 2018 and February 2019, complainants and other Agency officials repeatedly informed senior leadership that Tribal team members were subjected to hostile and discriminatory treatment by representatives of an Agency contractor.

Despite these repeated notifications, senior leadership condoned the contractors' conduct and continued to place the Tribal team in situations involving hostile interactions with contracting officials.
## PUBLIC RECOGNITION OMISSION
On May 5, 2019, the Agency issued a public statement via social media thanking local, state, and federal workers for their dedication and service in connection with their work.
However, the Agency failed to acknowledge or reference the Tribal team members, despite their substantial contributions to the same initiatives.
## ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS
Following the completion of investigations, the complainants received copies of their investigative files and requested hearings before EEOC Administrative Judges.
The complaints were assigned to different Administrative Judges within the Commission's Washington Field Office.
Complainants' legal representative filed motions to consolidate the complaints for joint processing before each judge.
The Agency opposed these consolidation motions.
One Administrative Judge denied the consolidation motion while the other judge did not issue a ruling on the motion.
Both judges subsequently issued separate summary judgment decisions concluding that no discrimination or unlawful retaliation had been established.
The Agency implemented the Administrative Judges' decisions as its final action.
Both complainants subsequently filed appeals challenging these determinations.
# CASE FILE RECORD: EEO DISCRIMINATION COMPLAINT
## CASE OVERVIEW

This case involves an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint filed by an Aircraft Mechanic employed at the Agency's Aircraft Maintenance Squadron facility located at Robins Air Force Base, Georgia.
The complainant alleged that he was subjected to a hostile work environment based on his protected status characteristics including race (African-American), color (Black), and age (52 years old).
## PARTIES AND POSITIONS OF AUTHORITY
At the time of the alleged incident, the complainant worked under the direct supervision of an Aircraft Overhaul Supervisor, who served as his first-level supervisor.
The complainant's second-level supervisor was the Production Team Lead.
The hierarchical structure is documented in the original Report of Investigation.
## FACTUAL BACKGROUND OF THE INCIDENT
On December 11, 2020, the complainant sustained a work-related injury resulting in a bleeding head wound.
The complainant left his work area in an attempt to locate a bandage to treat the wound.
During this time, his immediate supervisor observed him away from his assigned work station.
Upon discovering the complainant, the supervisor began verbally assaulting him, utilizing profane and demeaning language.

Specifically, the supervisor shouted the following statement: "Get your ass back on the plane, you do not do shit every day, I want you off my fucking team immediately, and I am tired of your shit." Additionally, the complainant alleged that the supervisor refused to provide first aid assistance for his head injury.
Following this incident, the complainant reported the matter to his second-level supervisor and another Agency official.
The complainant did not initially attribute the supervisor's conduct to discriminatory motives based on age or race.
## EEO COMPLAINT AND INVESTIGATION PROCEDURE
On May 25, 2021, the complainant formally filed an EEO complaint with the Agency alleging hostile work environment discrimination.

The Agency conducted an investigation and subsequently provided the complainant with a copy of the investigation report along with notification of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ).
## ADMINISTRATIVE JUDGE'S DECISION
The complainant timely requested a hearing.
On January 21, 2022, the AJ issued a Notice of Proposed Summary Judgment, outlining the relevant case facts and preliminary findings.
The AJ noted that while the supervisor's conduct was unprofessional and unacceptable, it did not constitute harassment under applicable law.
The AJ characterized the incident as an isolated occurrence in which the supervisor lost his temper while using facially neutral language.
The cursing, though inappropriate, was deemed insufficient to establish the severity required to support a hostile work environment claim.
The AJ offered both parties an opportunity to respond to the proposed summary judgment.

In his response, the complainant introduced new allegations for the first time, asserting without supporting evidence that the supervisor harbored a history of hatred toward him and had mistreated other African-American employees.
The complainant further alleged that the supervisor had made comments regarding President Obama and displayed Confederate flag imagery within the hangar.
These new allegations had not been previously included in the EEO Counselor Report, the formal complaint, or the complainant's affidavit.
The Agency did not timely respond to the proposed summary judgment notice but did submit documentation of the supervisor's disciplinary suspension.
On February 25, 2022, the AJ issued a final decision without holding a hearing, adopting the proposed summary judgment.
The decision noted that the complainant had initially reported not believing the incident was motivated by race or age.
Given the totality of circumstances presented, the AJ concluded that the complainant failed to establish discrimination as alleged.
The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ's finding.
## DISCIPLINARY ACTION TAKEN

Following investigation of the incident, the Agency imposed disciplinary measures against the supervisor, including a ten-day suspension without pay, reassignment to day shift operations, and a ninety-day restriction from supervisory duties.
The supervisor's role as the complainant's supervisor terminated immediately following the incident.
## CURRENT APPEAL CONTENTIONS
The complainant has appealed the AJ's decision, contending that he was subjected to humiliation, intimidation, bullying, and racist treatment.
He maintains that he provided investigators with a detailed list of racially motivated incidents and corresponding witnesses.

The complainant further argues that discrimination allegations were raised multiple times prior to summary judgment and that the Agency has withheld vital information regarding the supervisor's history that would demonstrate a pattern of racial discrimination against African-American employees.
The complainant asserts that the summary judgment decision denied him the opportunity to obtain such information.
The Agency maintains that the AJ's summary judgment decision was procedurally and substantively proper and should be upheld.

# INVESTIGATION RECORD - CASE FILE DOCUMENTATION
## Case Background and Complaint Filing
The complainant, employed as an Administrative Technician at the GS-0303-05 level, worked at the Agency's Chicago Regional Office located in Oak Brook, Illinois.

On August 24, 2021, the complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint asserting that the Agency had engaged in discriminatory and retaliatory conduct resulting in his termination, which became effective on July 28, 2021.
The complainant alleged that discrimination was based on his disabilities, specifically diabetes and liver fibrosis.
Additionally, he claimed the Agency retaliated against him for engaging in protected EEO activity by requesting reasonable accommodations.
The complainant did not challenge the framing or characterization of his complaint.
## Investigation and Agency Decision Process

Following completion of the investigation, the Agency provided the complainant with a copy of the investigation report and formal notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge.
The complainant exercised his right to request such a hearing.
Subsequently, the Agency issued a final decision in accordance with 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b), concluding that the complainant failed to establish that the Agency had subjected him to discrimination as alleged in his complaint.
This final decision prompted the complainant to file the instant appeal.
## Agency's Findings Regarding Disability Status
The Agency's final decision acknowledged and accepted certain factual findings.
Specifically, the Agency determined that the complainant was indeed an individual with a disability under applicable law and that he qualified for protection under the Rehabilitation Act.

However, while assuming arguendo that the complainant had established a prima facie case of both discrimination and retaliation, the Agency concluded that it had articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the complainant's termination that the complainant failed to rebut as pretextual.
## Employment History and Performance Issues
The complainant began employment with the Agency on January 17, 2021, under a Competitive-Career Conditional Appointment, which subjected him to a mandatory one-year probationary period.
Prior to this appointment, the complainant had worked for the Agency in an excepted service position as an Administrative Manager during the decennial census operations.
During his tenure, several supervisors documented performance concerns.
A progress review dated June 15, 2021, prepared by the complainant's first-level supervisor, indicated that he was not performing at the fully successful level 3 or above.
The review identified specific areas requiring improvement, including familiarization with onboarding procedures and payroll processes, as well as timely completion of work assignments.
Additional performance issues emerged in June 2021.

The complainant's third-level supervisor (S3), a Program Coordinator, sent three separate emails addressing performance deficiencies related to incomplete or missing compensation for two employees, delayed payroll processing for pay period 11, and the status of newly hired staff members.
On June 17, 2021, this supervisor issued a memorandum explicitly titled "Failure to Follow Up on Payroll Issues," further documenting the complainant's performance deficiencies.
## Operational Impact and Supervisory Observations

Another first-level supervisor (S1), an Administrative Officer, provided an affidavit detailing how the complainant's errors resulted in incorrect or delayed compensation for multiple employees, which ultimately led to newly hired staff resigning from their positions.
When S1 assumed supervisory responsibility in early July 2021, she initiated retraining of the affected staff members.
Despite this retraining intervention, S1 documented that the complainant continued to experience unresolved pay issues affecting the new hires under his responsibility.
## Termination and Stated Reasons
The complainant received his termination letter on July 28, 2021, from S3.
The letter cited unacceptable performance during the probationary period as the basis for termination.
Specifically, the letter identified the complainant's failure to ensure timely onboarding of new hires and proper tracking throughout the hiring process.
Additionally, the letter noted his failure to process payroll in a timely and accurate manner.
## Contrasting Supervisory Observations

An Administrative Specialist (AS) provided testimony indicating she had supervised the complainant during portions of his tenure, specifically regarding tasks related to the Census Investigative Service Missing Documents Project rather than payroll and timekeeping responsibilities.

This supervisor averred that she did not observe any unacceptable job performance issues related to the complainant's work on the Missing Documents Project and that no such concerns were brought to her attention.

The Administrative Specialist further expressed her personal belief that the complainant's termination was based on his disabilities and his request for reasonable accommodations, citing observed tension between the complainant and S3 regarding work schedule arrangements.
## Agency's Resolution of Conflicting Evidence

The Agency found that the legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the complainant's probationary termination were grounded in documented performance deficiencies related to payroll processing and new hire onboarding procedures, which the complainant frequently failed to complete without errors or in a timely manner.

In evaluating whether the complainant successfully demonstrated pretext, the Agency acknowledged the Administrative Specialist's affidavit but determined that her limited supervisory scope—covering only the Missing Documents Project—did not extend to timekeeping and payroll responsibilities.

The Agency noted that three supervisors had confirmed the complainant's deficiencies in the relevant areas, thereby finding that the Administrative Specialist's statements did not substantially undermine the Agency's explanation.
The Agency further noted the absence of evidence demonstrating that S3 had voiced opposition to the complainant's reasonable accommodation request or objected to his telework schedule.
The Agency observed that all Administrative Technicians supervised by S3 teleworked two days per week during the relevant period.
Consequently, the Agency concluded that the complainant could not demonstrate the Agency's reasons were pretextual, distinguishing between the complainant's subjective beliefs and objective evidence.

# INVESTIGATION RECORD - CASE FILE DOCUMENTATION
## COMPLAINANT INFORMATION AND EMPLOYMENT STATUS

At the time of the events that precipitated this complaint, the Complainant was employed as a Supervisory Transportation Security Officer at the pay grade SV-1802-G Band at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Atlanta, Georgia.

On February 2, 2021, the Complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint with the Agency alleging unlawful discrimination and creation of a hostile work environment based on sex (male) and in retaliation for prior protected EEO activity.
## ALLEGATIONS AND FACTUAL BASIS
The complaint encompasses four primary allegations spanning a three-month period from November through December 2020:

**Allegation One:** On November 24, 2020, a coworker (hereinafter referred to as CW1) allegedly claimed to practice Voodoo and placed a flower on the Complainant's body without authorization or consent.

**Allegation Two:** Following the November 24, 2020 incident, Agency management allegedly failed to adequately address the Complainant's concerns regarding CW1's conduct, prevented him from attending certain management meetings, and restricted his participation in scheduling operational meetings.

**Allegation Three:** On December 30, 2020, a manager (hereinafter referred to as Manager) allegedly engaged in intimidating conduct by pacing back and forth, standing directly over the Complainant, and physically blocking the door when the Complainant attempted to leave the area.
In support of these allegations, the Complainant stated that he had requested CW1 to maintain distance and cease her behavior, but she refused and allegedly backed him into a corner.
The Complainant reported that he submitted complaints to Agency management on November 24 and November 28, 2020, but received no corrective action.
## INVESTIGATION AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY
On December 21, 2020, the Interim Federal Security Director appointed Manager to investigate the Complainant's allegations.
The Complainant subsequently objected to this appointment, contending that Manager was part of his direct management chain and therefore possessed an inherent conflict of interest.

During the investigation process, the Complainant alleged that Manager refused to provide proper documentation of his investigative authority and deliberately prevented the Complainant from viewing the authorizing memorandum on Manager's computer.
In response to these concerns, on January 5, 2021, the Federal Security Director appointed a Transportation Security Inspector to assume investigative responsibility.
The Complainant agreed to cooperate with the Inspector's investigation.
## INSPECTOR'S FINDINGS
On January 22, 2021, the Inspector issued a comprehensive fact-finding report concluding that the Complainant's allegations could not be substantiated.
The investigation included interviews with the Complainant, CW1, and several coworkers who worked in the same operational area.

The Inspector acknowledged that a "contentious conversation" occurred between the Complainant and CW1, but the parties offered conflicting accounts regarding the substance and initiation of the exchange.
The Complainant maintained that CW1 requested private conversation and subsequently cornered him.
CW1 provided contradictory testimony, asserting that the Complainant initiated the conversation and questioned her regarding her relationship with another employee, which she found upsetting.
Coworkers confirmed that a conversation transpired but could not substantiate the specific details or allegations made by either party.
The Inspector noted that much of the evidence gathered consisted of "conjecture" rather than verifiable facts.
No physical evidence was recovered, and witness accounts remained inconclusive.
## COMPLAINANT'S POSITION AND EVIDENCE ASSESSMENT

The Complainant contended that the totality of circumstances revealed a discriminatory pattern, arguing that female employees were not subjected to comparable discipline while male employees experienced harsher treatment.
He characterized the investigation as biased and insufficient, asserting that security footage would have corroborated his version of events.
The Complainant expressed dissatisfaction with the investigation's scope and conclusions, stating it failed to address his concerns or mitigate the alleged discriminatory conduct.
CW1 submitted an affidavit reaffirming her original statements and denying the Complainant's characterization of events.
Coworker statements remained consistent with their investigative interviews, confirming a contentious interaction but providing no corroborating details.
## FINAL AGENCY DECISION AND APPEAL
Following completion of the investigation, the Agency provided the Complainant with the investigative report and notice of hearing rights before an EEO Administrative Judge.
Pursuant to the Complainant's request, the Agency issued a final decision under 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b), finding that the Complainant was not subjected to discrimination or retaliation as alleged.
The Complainant subsequently appealed this determination.

# INVESTIGATION RECORD AND ADMINISTRATIVE DECISION
## CASE BACKGROUND AND COMPLAINANT STATUS

This case involves a formal employment discrimination complaint filed by an individual employed as a City Carrier Technician, Classification A-02/Q, at the Agency's Village Station located in New York, New York.

At the time of the events giving rise to this complaint, the Complainant performed duties consistent with her position classification, which included casing and delivering mail for multiple carrier routes.
The standard job duties required employees in this position to engage in pushing, lifting, and simple grasping activities on a daily basis for the full eight-hour workday.
These physical demands would become central to the subsequent allegations and investigation findings.
## ALLEGATIONS AND CLAIMS
The Complainant raised three distinct claims of discrimination and/or improper personnel action.

First, she alleged that beginning June 26, 2016, and continuing thereafter, management personnel assigned her to work duties that fell outside the scope of her documented medical restrictions and failed to compensate her properly or timely for hours worked.
Second, she alleged that on October 4, 2016, and on other unspecified dates, her electronic clock ring records were improperly deleted from the timekeeping system.
Third, she alleged that her requests to be detailed to a 204-B supervisory position were denied without legitimate justification.
## MEDICAL HISTORY AND RESTRICTIONS
The Complainant's medical conditions originated from an on-the-job injury initially diagnosed on May 10, 2014.
Following this injury, she developed a back sprain, displacement of a lumbar intervertebral disc without myelopathy, and a hernia, which required surgical repair.
Due to these conditions, her treating physician imposed comprehensive medical restrictions on her work activities.
These restrictions limited her sitting to three hours per day, walking to a maximum of thirty minutes, and standing to only ten minutes.
Additionally, she was restricted from reaching above shoulder level, twisting, bending, stooping, pushing, pulling, lifting, squatting, kneeling, and climbing.
To accommodate these limitations, she required fifteen-minute rest breaks every hour during her workday.
## MODIFIED JOB ASSIGNMENT AND ACCOMMODATION EFFORTS
Following an extended leave of absence, the Complainant was initially assigned to the Lenox Hill Station.
On June 22, 2016, management offered her a limited-duty modified assignment at the Lenox Hill South Station.

This position involved shuttling carriers via van to and from their assigned routes and delivering express mail packages weighing under five pounds for a maximum of four hours daily and up to thirty minutes of express mail delivery work.
The assignment was offered on a part-time basis, with hours scheduled from 10:00 a.m.
to 2:00 p.m.
This position was not a vacant, funded position within the standard organizational structure.
On its face, the offered assignment appeared to align with her documented medical restrictions.
The Complainant signed the modified job offer on July 1, 2016, and commenced the assignment on or about July 18, 2016.
During initial discussions regarding the position, the Complainant expressed concerns about her ability to perform the work.
However, she indicated her willingness to attempt the assignment, with an understanding that she would notify her Manager if she proved unable to sustain the duties.
Her Manager agreed to this arrangement.

The Manager later testified that he became aware of the Complainant's medical condition solely through the job offer documentation and stated that he did not receive or possess any separate medical documentation detailing her specific restrictions.
Management also offered the Complainant an alternative accommodation: a lobby attendant position.
The Complainant declined this opportunity, believing that the duties associated with that position would exceed her medical capabilities given her documented restrictions.
## ASSIGNMENT AND WORK INCIDENT
Despite the apparent alignment between the modified assignment and her restrictions, the Complainant maintained reservations about her ability to perform the work.
On August 29, 2016, the Manager provided instructions for the Complainant to make an express mail delivery, which he believed conformed to her restrictions.
However, the Complainant reported that she walked for approximately one hour during this shift, including scheduled breaks, which exceeded her thirty-minute walking restriction.
The Complainant indicated that she was not permitted to use the van for transportation between delivery points.
She noted that using the van, as contemplated in the modified job offer, would require stooping and twisting to enter the vehicle—activities prohibited by her medical restrictions.
She provided the additional example that even retrieving an envelope that fell to the ground would constitute a violation of her stooping restriction.
## TIMEKEEPING AND COMPENSATION ISSUES
The investigation revealed that the Complainant was on extended leave during July and August 2016.
Electronic clock ring records for the period from July 18, 2016, through July 28, 2016, had been deleted from the timekeeping system, with her hours coded as full workers' compensation.
Given that the Complainant had recently commenced work at the Lenox Hill South Station, the receiving facility should have been responsible for entering her time into the system.
The Manager asserted that an incorrect leave code had been entered into the system for this period, explaining the data discrepancy.
The Complainant did not return to work until October 4, 2016, at which time she returned specifically to complete workers' compensation paperwork.
She made an additional appearance on November 14, 2016, to complete supplemental paperwork.

The investigation identified a critical procedural issue: because the Complainant had recently transitioned from full-time workers' compensation status and had been transferred from the Village Station to the Lenox Hill facility, supervisory personnel at the receiving facility may not have realized she had returned to active work status.
This lack of awareness at the receiving facility likely contributed to the timekeeping errors.
During the investigation, it was further determined that manual timecards had been submitted and subsequently lost, rather than being entered digitally.
A digital submission system would have prevented such losses.
The Complainant herself acknowledged that her Manager's organizational deficiencies may have contributed to some of the errors that occurred.

The Agency maintained that all payment failures resulted from administrative error rather than intentional misconduct.
## 204-B DETAIL REQUEST
The Complainant asserted that she had requested a detail assignment as a 204-B acting supervisor to supervise other carriers.
She indicated that on or about November 14, 2016, the Manager declined to offer her a 204-B detail as a reasonable accommodation.
The Manager stated that he had no operational need for additional acting supervisors at that time.
Furthermore, he expressed his belief that supervisory positions require punctuality and reliability—characteristics he did not observe in the Complainant based on her attendance record.
## ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING AND DECISION
Following the completion of the investigation, the Agency provided the Complainant with a copy of the investigative report and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Administrative Judge.
The Complainant timely exercised this right.
The assigned Administrative Judge issued a summary judgment decision finding in favor of the Agency on all claims.

Regarding the denial of reasonable accommodation claim, the Administrative Judge determined that the Complainant had been offered a modified limited-duty assignment involving van shuttling and express mail delivery that fell within her documented restrictions.
The Administrative Judge noted that while the Complainant believed the assignment exceeded her capabilities, no objective evidence demonstrated that she was forced to work outside her restrictions.
The Agency had offered a second accommodation—the lobby attendant position—which the Complainant declined.

The Administrative Judge concluded that the Complainant appeared unable to perform her job with or without reasonable accommodation given the severity of her medical restrictions, and therefore found no violation of the Rehabilitation Act.
On the remaining claims, the Administrative Judge found that the Agency had articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions.

Regarding compensation and timekeeping issues, the Administrative Judge accepted the Agency's explanation that multiple administrative factors contributed to the errors, including the Complainant's status transition from workers' compensation, her facility transfer, the loss of manual timecards, and the Manager's organizational deficiencies.

Concerning the 204-B detail denial, the Administrative Judge determined that the Complainant sought immediate promotion without participating in the standard application process, and she failed to demonstrate that discrimination or retaliation motivated the Manager's decision.
The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully adopting the Administrative Judge's decision.
The Complainant has appealed this determination.

# CASE FILE INVESTIGATION RECORD
## Case Summary and Background
This matter concerns employment discrimination allegations brought by a Deportation Officer (DO), GS-12, formerly employed at the Agency's San Bernardino, California office.

The complainant, born in 1971 and of Romanian national origin, filed an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) complaint on June 6, 2019, alleging unlawful discrimination and hostile work environment treatment.

The allegations were based on his national origin, age, and claimed reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967.
## Supervisory Relationship and Personnel Context

At the time of the events giving rise to this complaint, the complainant's first-line supervisor was a Supervisory Detention and Deportation Officer of Vietnamese national origin, born in 1977, with no prior EEO activity on record.
The complainant had no prior EEO complaints before the incidents at issue.
Additionally, a second Deportation Officer (DO 2), born in 1969 and possessing prior EEO activity history, was also involved in certain aspects of this investigation.
## Factual Circumstances
### Schedule Adjustment Request – July 26-27, 2018
The first significant event occurred when the complainant requested adjustment of his work schedule to accommodate attendance at a recreational concert with his daughter.
On July 27, 2018, the complainant allegedly submitted a text message to his supervisor requesting modification of his schedule from the standard hours to 0500-1300 hours.
According to the supervisor's account, he denied this specific request but offered alternative accommodations: either an earlier start time of 0600 hours or the option to use annual leave.
The supervisor recalled that the complainant indicated via text that he would take leave; however, the complainant subsequently reported to work as scheduled.
The parties' accounts regarding whether this constituted disparate treatment formed the basis of the complainant's first allegation.
### Scheduling and Overtime Dispute – July 27, 2018
Concurrent with the schedule adjustment discussion, the supervisor asserted that he asked the complainant to return to his office during the complainant's duty hours.
According to the supervisor's statement, the complainant continued working his remaining scheduled hours and subsequently worked overtime from 4:30 p.m.
until 7:00 p.m.
The complainant, however, claimed that the supervisor asked him to return to work after he had already left for the day.

The complainant's timekeeping records reflected work hours spanning 0500 to 1900 hours on this date, comprising eight hours of regular pay and six hours of Administrative Uncontrollable Overtime (AUO).
This discrepancy regarding the nature and authorization of the overtime became relevant to subsequent pay adjustment disputes.
### Defensive Tactics Training – August 28, 2018
On August 28, 2018, the complainant attended an all-day Defensive Tactics training class scheduled from 8:00 a.m.
to 4:00 p.m.
This training date subsequently became significant in the context of AUO pay calculations, as the complainant claimed he had worked AUO hours from 3:00 p.m.
to 5:00 p.m.
on the same date.
### Pay Discrepancy Allegations – October 1, 2018
The complainant asserted that on October 1, 2018, he became aware of pay discrepancies allegedly made by his supervisor.
Additionally, the complainant claimed that the supervisor had previously informed DO 2 of DO 2's AUO pay discrepancy before correcting DO 2's compensation, suggesting differential treatment.
The supervisor acknowledged discovering an AUO discrepancy affecting the complainant's August 28, 2018 timesheet.
The supervisor explained that because the complainant was in training from 3:00 p.m.
to 4:00 p.m., that hour was excludable from AUO calculations and therefore could not be claimed as overtime.
Consequently, the supervisor had made the appropriate pay adjustment to reflect this exclusion.
The supervisor noted that DO 2 had been available in the office when the supervisor discovered DO 2's AUO discrepancy, which enabled direct discussion with DO 2 regarding the adjustment.
### Performance Work Plan Review – October 12, 2018
On October 12, 2018, the supervisor conducted a performance review meeting with the complainant regarding his Performance Work Plan (PWP).
The complainant alleged that the supervisor admonished him multiple times within the PWP and rated him on performance elements not included in his official PWP.

The supervisor maintained that he did not rate the complainant on elements outside those contained in the official PWP, noting that he evaluated the complainant on the following elements: Plans and Conducts Arrest, Custody Operations, Deportation, Partnering, and Prepares Reports and Other Correspondence.
According to the supervisor, the complainant became upset during this meeting, walked away, and declined to engage in further discussion of the performance matters.
## EEO Complaint Process
The complainant initiated EEO contact on October 12, 2018, immediately following the PWP review meeting.

The formal EEO complaint was filed on June 6, 2019, encompassing four discrete incidents and claiming discrimination based on national origin (Romanian), age (48 years old), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity referenced in complaints HS-ICE-21417-2012 and HS-ICE-22663-2012.
## Investigation and Hearing Process
The Agency conducted a comprehensive investigation into the allegations.
Upon completion of the investigation, the complainant received the investigative report and was notified of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ).
The complainant timely requested such a hearing.
However, significant procedural complications arose when the complainant failed to provide a completed investigative affidavit despite multiple requests from the EEO investigator.
The AJ issued an Order to Show Good Cause on June 7, 2021, directing the complainant to explain his failure to comply.
When the complainant failed to submit the affidavit by the AJ's May 11, 2021 order, the AJ provided an additional opportunity for the complainant to explain the non-compliance by June 17, 2021.
On June 21, 2021, the complainant emailed the AJ with apologies but still failed to provide the required affidavit.
Consequently, on June 22, 2021, the AJ dismissed the complaint from the EEOC hearing process as a sanction for non-compliance and remanded the matter to the Agency to issue a Final Agency Decision.
## Final Agency Decision Analysis
On August 10, 2021, the Agency issued its Final Agency Decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
The Agency applied the three-part McDonnell Douglas evidentiary framework from McDonnell Douglas Corp.
v.
Green, 411 U.S.
792 (1973), to analyze the disparate treatment allegations in claims 1, 3, and 4.
The Agency determined that management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for each challenged action.

For claim 1 (schedule denial), the Agency noted the supervisor's statement that the complainant chose to report to work rather than use leave and received no differential treatment compared to other officers.

For claim 3 (pay discrepancy notification), the Agency found that the supervisor explained his different communication approach by noting DO 2's office availability at the time of the discrepancy discovery.
For claim 4 (PWP rating), the Agency concluded that the supervisor did not rate the complainant on elements outside his official PWP.

The Agency found the complainant failed to prove by preponderance of evidence that the legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons were pretexts for discrimination or that any Agency actions were motivated by protected class membership.

Regarding the hostile work environment and remaining claims, the Agency applied harassment standards, concluding the complainant failed to demonstrate that management actions were motivated by discriminatory intent or based on protected class membership.
The Agency found the alleged conduct did not rise to the level of severe or pervasive harassment contemplated by Title VII, nor was any conduct demonstrably based on protected status.
This appeal followed, though neither party submitted supplemental appeal statements for consideration.

# INVESTIGATION CASE FILE RECORD
## COMPLAINANT AND EMPLOYMENT BACKGROUND
At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, the Complainant was employed as a Customs and Border Protection Officer (CBPO) at the U.S.
Customs and Border Protection Agency's San Ysidro Port of Entry located in San Ysidro, California.

The Complainant, born in 1954, filed this complaint alleging discrimination based on age under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA) and retaliation for prior protected Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
## ALLEGATIONS OF HARASSMENT AND ADVERSE ACTIONS
### Initial Counseling and Management Actions
Beginning May 31, 2018, the Complainant alleged he was subjected to ongoing harassment.
On that date, the Branch Chief refused to rescind a Memorandum of Counseling the Complainant had received regarding his use of the Treasury Enforcement Communication System (TECS).

According to Agency documentation, the Branch Chief had requested the issuance of this memorandum after the Complainant was instructed twice not to place the terms "E/O if not in vehicle" on TECS records, as such notations create system violations.
Despite these explicit instructions, the Complainant continued this practice, prompting the corrective action.
### Allegations of Bullying and Supervisory Harassment

From February 2019 through June 2019, the Complainant alleged that his Supervisory CBP Officer (identified as SCBPO-1) engaged in bullying and harassment, with the Branch Chief remaining aware of this conduct yet taking no corrective measures.
Specific incidents cited include:
On April 17, 2019, SCBPO-1 verbally reprimanded the Complainant for missing a morning training class.
In June 2019, SCBPO-1 displayed a knife to the Complainant and another CBPO (CBPO-2), indicating he regularly brings his knife collection to work in his backpack.
On June 3, 2019, SCBPO-1 sent the Complainant an email reprimand concerning his TECS access expiration.
### Schedule Change and Birthday Celebration Incident
On June 19, 2019, SCBPO-1 altered the Complainant's work schedule from 2:00 p.m.
to 1:00 p.m.
to 9:00 p.m.
to accommodate a celebration for the Branch Chief's birthday.
During this incident, SCBPO-1 solicited twenty dollars from the Complainant for the birthday party.
### Reassignment and Leave Approval Issues

On or around August 16, 2019, SCBPO-1 and another Supervisory CBP Officer (SCBPO-2) informed the Complainant's coworkers that he would be reassigned and leaving the Intelligence Targeting Unit effective September 1, 2019, although no actual reassignment occurred at that time.
On the same date, these supervisors informed the Complainant that his requested leave for September 2019 would not be approved.
However, following the Complainant's inquiry regarding this decision, his leave request was ultimately approved.
### Removal from Detail
Effective March 8, 2020, the Complainant was formally removed from his detail in the Intelligence Targeting Unit (ITU).
## INVESTIGATIVE FINDINGS AND AGENCY RESPONSES
### Dismissed Claims
The Agency dismissed two separate claims.
First, a claim regarding the Complainant's non-receipt of a year-end monetary award, which he learned about on December 23, 2018.
Second, a claim involving SCBPO-1 charging the Complainant with one hour of Leave Without Pay on April 21, 2019, for untimely counselor contact.

Additionally, the Agency dismissed three claims alleging that SCBPO-1 spoke unprofessionally about coworkers, finding these claims failed to establish that the Complainant was aggrieved by comments made about other employees.
### Agency Explanations for Challenged Actions

The Intelligence Division Chief provided explanations for the TECS-related counseling, stating that the Complainant had requested that CBPOs "exempt" travelers on primary who had illegal activity links or ties, or whom he had targeted for illegal activity.
This action constituted a request to violate TECS policy.
The Chief approved the Memorandum of Counseling due to the Complainant's failure to follow explicit instructions despite being asked twice to comply.

Regarding the June 3, 2019 email regarding TECS access, SCBPO-1 explained that the TECS system sends automated periodic reminders when recertification is required, commencing thirty days before the certification due date.

SCBPO-1 stated he received an automated system notification that the Complainant had lost access and subsequently sent a counseling email reminding the Complainant of his obligation to maintain active TECS access.
### Birthday Celebration Explanation
SCBPO-1 explained that the Intelligence Targeting Unit maintained a tradition of organizing potlucks or obtaining catering for group events, with participation announced as optional.
He stated that employees were asked to donate ten dollars if they wished to participate.
According to his account, CBPO-2 provided twenty dollars to cover both his own participation and the Complainant's after the Complainant verbally indicated his desire to participate.
### Removal from Intelligence Targeting Unit
The Intelligence Division Chief explained that the Complainant was removed from his ITU detail due to his failure to perform basic duties as an ITU officer.
Specifically, a Watch Commander contacted the Complainant requesting assistance on a particular case and sought an expeditious response.
The Complainant failed to perform the requested task and instead delegated the assignment to other members of the Tactical Terrorism Response Team.
## PROCEDURAL HISTORY AND AFFIDAVIT SUBMISSION
During the investigation process, the Complainant was provided two weeks to submit an affidavit but requested two weeks of administrative or sick leave to complete this document.
On September 28, 2020, one day before the original deadline, the investigator granted an extension and approved sixteen hours of administrative leave for September 23-24, 2020.
Despite these accommodations, the Complainant failed to submit an affidavit.
## AGENCY FINAL DECISION

The Agency's final decision found that the Complainant failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination, noting the absence of evidence that employees outside his protected classes received differential treatment.
The Agency further articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for all challenged actions and found no evidence of discriminatory animus.
The decision concluded that the Complainant did not establish that alleged harassment incidents were motivated by his protected class status and therefore failed to prove discrimination as alleged.
## APPEAL AND CURRENT STATUS
The Complainant appealed the Agency's decision, contending that the investigation was inadequate and requesting referral to an Administrative Judge for additional investigation.
He also asserted that the Agency's stated reasons were untrue.
The Agency responded that the Complainant received adequate time to submit his affidavit but failed to do so and submitted no evidence supporting allegations of discriminatory animus.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, the Complainant was not employed as a Customs and Border Protection Officer (CBPO) at the U.S.
Customs and Border Protection Agency's San Ysidro Port of Entry located in San Ysidro, California.

The Complainant, born in 1954, filed this complaint alleging discrimination based on age under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA) and retaliation for prior protected Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
## ALLEGATIONS OF HARASSMENT AND ADVERSE ACTIONS
### Initial Counseling and Management Actions
Beginning May 31, 2018, the Complainant alleged he was subjected to ongoing harassment.
On that date, the Branch Chief refused to rescind a Memorandum of Counseling the Complainant had received regarding his use of the Treasury Enforcement Communication System (TECS).

According to Agency documentation, the Branch Chief had requested the issuance of this memorandum after the Complainant was instructed twice not to place the terms "E/O if not in vehicle" on TECS records, as such notations create system violations.
Despite these explicit instructions, the Complainant continued this practice, prompting the corrective action.
### Allegations of Bullying and Supervisory Harassment

From February 2019 through June 2019, the Complainant alleged that his Supervisory CBP Officer (identified as SCBPO-1) engaged in bullying and harassment, with the Branch Chief remaining aware of this conduct yet taking no corrective measures.
Specific incidents cited include:
On April 17, 2019, SCBPO-1 verbally reprimanded the Complainant for missing a morning training class.
In June 2019, SCBPO-1 displayed a knife to the Complainant and another CBPO (CBPO-2), indicating he regularly brings his knife collection to work in his backpack.
On June 3, 2019, SCBPO-1 sent the Complainant an email reprimand concerning his TECS access expiration.
### Schedule Change and Birthday Celebration Incident
On June 19, 2019, SCBPO-1 altered the Complainant's work schedule from 2:00 p.m.
to 1:00 p.m.
to 9:00 p.m.
to accommodate a celebration for the Branch Chief's birthday.
During this incident, SCBPO-1 solicited twenty dollars from the Complainant for the birthday party.
### Reassignment and Leave Approval Issues

On or around August 16, 2019, SCBPO-1 and another Supervisory CBP Officer (SCBPO-2) informed the Complainant's coworkers that he would be reassigned and leaving the Intelligence Targeting Unit effective September 1, 2019, although no actual reassignment occurred at that time.
On the same date, these supervisors informed the Complainant that his requested leave for September 2019 would not be approved.
However, following the Complainant's inquiry regarding this decision, his leave request was ultimately approved.
### Removal from Detail
Effective March 8, 2020, the Complainant was formally removed from his detail in the Intelligence Targeting Unit (ITU).
## INVESTIGATIVE FINDINGS AND AGENCY RESPONSES
### Dismissed Claims
The Agency dismissed two separate claims.
First, a claim regarding the Complainant's non-receipt of a year-end monetary award, which he learned about on December 23, 2018.
Second, a claim involving SCBPO-1 charging the Complainant with one hour of Leave Without Pay on April 21, 2019, for untimely counselor contact.

Additionally, the Agency dismissed three claims alleging that SCBPO-1 spoke unprofessionally about coworkers, finding these claims failed to establish that the Complainant was aggrieved by comments made about other employees.
### Agency Explanations for Challenged Actions

The Intelligence Division Chief provided explanations for the TECS-related counseling, stating that the Complainant had requested that CBPOs "exempt" travelers on primary who had illegal activity links or ties, or whom he had targeted for illegal activity.
This action constituted a request to violate TECS policy.
The Chief approved the Memorandum of Counseling due to the Complainant's failure to follow explicit instructions despite being asked twice to comply.

Regarding the June 3, 2019 email regarding TECS access, SCBPO-1 explained that the TECS system sends automated periodic reminders when recertification is required, commencing thirty days before the certification due date.

SCBPO-1 stated he received an automated system notification that the Complainant had lost access and subsequently sent a counseling email reminding the Complainant of his obligation to maintain active TECS access.
### Birthday Celebration Explanation
SCBPO-1 explained that the Intelligence Targeting Unit maintained a tradition of organizing potlucks or obtaining catering for group events, with participation announced as optional.
He stated that employees were asked to donate ten dollars if they wished to participate.
According to his account, CBPO-2 provided twenty dollars to cover both his own participation and the Complainant's after the Complainant verbally indicated his desire to participate.
### Removal from Intelligence Targeting Unit
The Intelligence Division Chief explained that the Complainant was removed from his ITU detail due to his failure to perform basic duties as an ITU officer.
Specifically, a Watch Commander contacted the Complainant requesting assistance on a particular case and sought an expeditious response.
The Complainant failed to perform the requested task and instead delegated the assignment to other members of the Tactical Terrorism Response Team.
## PROCEDURAL HISTORY AND AFFIDAVIT SUBMISSION
During the investigation process, the Complainant was provided two weeks to submit an affidavit but requested two weeks of administrative or sick leave to complete this document.
On September 28, 2020, one day before the original deadline, the investigator granted an extension and approved sixteen hours of administrative leave for September 23-24, 2020.
Despite these accommodations, the Complainant failed to submit an affidavit.
## AGENCY FINAL DECISION

The Agency's final decision found that the Complainant failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination, noting the absence of evidence that employees outside his protected classes received differential treatment.
The Agency further articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for all challenged actions and found no evidence of discriminatory animus.
The decision concluded that the Complainant did not establish that alleged harassment incidents were motivated by his protected class status and therefore failed to prove discrimination as alleged.
## APPEAL AND CURRENT STATUS
The Complainant appealed the Agency's decision, contending that the investigation was inadequate and requesting referral to an Administrative Judge for additional investigation.
He also asserted that the Agency's stated reasons were untrue.
The Agency responded that the Complainant received adequate time to submit his affidavit but failed to do so and submitted no evidence supporting allegations of discriminatory animus.
# INVESTIGATION RECORD
## Case File Documentation
**Employee Status and Position:**
At the time of the events giving rise to this complaint, the Complainant was employed with the Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Agency as a CBP Officer, Grade GS-1895-12.
She was stationed at the El Paso Port of Entry in El Paso, Texas, within the Agency's El Paso Field Office under the Office of Field Operations division.
**Complaint Filing:**
On April 13, 2020, the Complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint with the Agency.

The complaint alleged hostile work environment and discrimination based on three protected characteristics: sex (female), disability (specifically cervical myelopathy and cervical fusion resulting in limited neck movement), and age (56 years old).
**Allegations and Timeline of Events:**
The complaint detailed a series of incidents spanning approximately four months, beginning in September 2019 and concluding in early February 2020.
The Complainant alleged that Supervisory CBP Officer designated as Supervisor 1 initiated a pattern of discriminatory behavior.

Between September 8, 2019, and January 2020, Supervisor 1 repeatedly assigned the Complainant regular cashier duties in addition to issuing I-94 documentation, despite the fact that the Complainant was on official Light Duty status.

In September 2019, Supervisor 1 expressed to the Program Manager an unwillingness to work with the Complainant in Passport Control Secondary, citing her Light Duty status and lack of weapon authorization as reasons.
On September 13, 2019, Supervisor 1 directly told the Complainant that she did not wish to work with her and characterized the Complainant as a liability due to her health conditions.

From October 2019 through February 2020, on approximately 10 to 15 separate occasions, Supervisor 1 interrupted conversations between the Complainant and coworkers, instructing them to cease communicating with her.
On December 24, 2019, Supervisor 1 assigned the Complainant to passport control duties despite her Light Duty restriction.

When the Complainant explained her limitations, Supervisor 1 responded dismissively with "it is what it is." Later that same day, in the presence of the public, Supervisor 1 yelled at the Complainant to begin issuing permits while loudly stating that the Complainant did not want to perform her job.
Supervisor 1 then addressed members of the public and invited them to file complaints against the Complainant for inadequate service.

On January 1 and 3, 2020, Supervisor 1 yelled at the Complainant, making accusations regarding unauthorized pat downs and case processing while on Light Duty, and alleged abuse of her light duty schedule.
On January 2, 2020, Supervisor 1 accused the Complainant of making false statements in a memorandum.
The Complainant's Light Duty shift was subsequently changed from 10:00 p.m.
to 6:00 a.m.
to midnight to 8:00 a.m.
for two days following a call from Supervisor 1 to the Chief.
On January 6, 2020, Supervisor 1 yelled at the Complainant by telephone, accusing her of working an incorrect schedule and refusing to perform her duties.

Between January 15 and 16, 2020, Supervisor 1 raised her tone, claimed the Complainant was unwilling to work, and threatened both verbal and written reprimands for failure to assume another officer's duties, as well as threatened discipline for insubordination.
A second supervisory officer, designated as Supervisor 2, also engaged in alleged discriminatory conduct.
On January 16, 2020, Supervisor 2 made derogatory comments and refused to initial an assignment, using profanity.
When the Complainant declined to perform cashier duties, Supervisor 2 made disparaging remarks about her value as an employee and ordered her to relocate within the office.
On January 31, 2020, both supervisors collaborated in directing the Complainant to perform cashier duties.
After Supervisor 1's involvement, Supervisor 2 reassigned the Complainant to detention log officer duties while raising his voice and demanding she vacate the work area.
Eventually, Supervisor 2 ordered the Complainant to go home on administrative leave.
**Subsequent Proceedings and Agency Decision:**

On February 6, 2020, the Complainant received formal notification of investigations against her, including accusations of unwillingness to work, disobedience, neglect of duties, and failure to obey directives.
She was afforded Weingarten rights and requested to provide a written statement.
Following investigation, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b), concluding that the Complainant failed to establish discrimination or disparate treatment as alleged in her complaint.
The Agency provided the Complainant with the investigation report and notice of her right to request an administrative hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge.

# INVESTIGATION RECORD
**Case File Summary: Employment Discrimination Investigation**
## Background and Employment Status

During the period under investigation, the Complainant was employed by the Agency as a Mail Handler in a Modified Assignment with Limited Duty status, classified as PS 4/P, at the Church Street Station location in New York, New York.
The Complainant was on an approved modified assignment due to a documented lumbosacral sprain.
During the specified period from July 5, 2019, through July 31, 2019, the Complainant was not permitted to work.
The Agency accepted the complaint for formal investigation, and the following pertinent facts were established through the investigative process.
## Union Grievance and Craft Assignment Issues
On June 15, 2019, the American Postal Workers Union, AFL-CIO, initiated a Step 2 grievance against the Agency.

The grievance alleged that the Complainant's assignment to perform Clerk Craft duties while maintaining her Modified Assignment status violated the collective bargaining agreement between the union and the Agency.
Specifically, the union contended that the assignment crossed craft lines, as it involved someone outside the Clerk Craft performing duties designated for Clerk Craft employees.

Documentation supporting this grievance, including the formal grievance filing, a union request for a detailed list of the Complainant's Modified Assignment duties, and affidavits from the Manager of Customer Services (identified as S2), who served as the Complainant's second-line supervisor, were included in the investigation record.
The Complainant did not dispute that she had performed Clerk Craft duties during her modified assignment.
## Medical Documentation Requests
On June 11, 2019, the Agency's Health & Resource Management (HRM) department contacted the Complainant.

The HRM office noted that her most recent medical documentation on file was dated January 18, 2011—more than eight years prior—and requested that she submit an updated medical note from her treating physician that included her current medical restrictions.
This request was reiterated on June 21, 2019.

According to statements from both S2 and the Complainant's first-line supervisor (identified as S1), the purpose of requesting updated medical documentation was to enable the Agency to draft a revised Modified Assignment that would align with her current medical restrictions while eliminating the craft-crossing issue identified in the union grievance.
Management sought to develop an assignment within appropriate craft lines and within the scope of her medical limitations.
Despite these requests, the Complainant refused to submit an updated doctor's note.
She believed the submission was unnecessary and declined to provide the documentation.
Subsequently, S2 directed the Complainant not to return to work until she provided an updated doctor's note describing her current medical restrictions.
The Complainant anticipated that once she submitted the updated medical documentation, she would be permitted to resume work.
## Submission of Medical Documentation
On July 5, 2019, the Complainant reported to work and submitted a medical letter dated July 2, 2019.

The doctor's letter contained the following restrictions: lifting, pushing and pulling not to exceed twenty pounds; reaching above shoulder height not to exceed twenty pounds; standing and walking for an average duration of twenty minutes.
According to S2's account, HRM determined that the submitted medical letter was insufficient because the limitations were not stated with adequate clarity.
S2 reported that he subsequently requested that the Complainant submit another updated doctor's letter providing more precise restrictions.
S1 corroborated that S2 had relayed this information to him, though S1 did not reference direct communication with HRM.
The Complainant ultimately submitted a revised doctor's note after July 31, 2019, and returned to work on August 1, 2019.
The HRM Manager stated that S2 had made the independent decision to prohibit the Complainant from working during this period.

The HRM Manager indicated that he became aware of this decision only after S2 implemented it and acknowledged that he was not initially informed of the rationale for Complainant's removal from the limited duty assignment.
## Management's Resolution and New Modified Assignment
On July 22, 2019, the HRM Manager sent correspondence to the Complainant indicating that the Agency was reviewing her Modified Assignment (Limited Duty) status.
This review was prompted by an arbitration award addressing the assignment of non-Clerk Craft employees to Clerk Craft duties.

The HRM Manager advised that management would conduct a search for appropriate and available work within her medical restrictions and would offer a revised Modified Assignment if suitable positions were identified.
On July 25, 2019, the HRM Manager presented the Complainant with a formal Offer of Modified Assignment (Limited Duty) to begin August 1, 2019.
The new position was Modified Handler (Modified Assignment – indefinite duration) at the James A.
Farley Retail Local Operation Center.
The job duties differed from her previous assignment.
Importantly, the Offer letter explicitly stated that the proposed duties fell within the restrictions outlined in her July 2, 2019 treating physician's letter.
The restrictions listed in the formal Offer were identical to those documented in her physician's letter.
## Administrative and Legal Proceedings
Following completion of the investigation, the Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge.
When the Complainant subsequently withdrew this request, the Administrative Judge directed the Agency to issue a Final Agency Decision (FAD).
In its FAD, the Agency concluded that no discrimination had occurred.
The Agency assumed, without making an explicit finding, that the Complainant constituted an individual with a disability.
However, the Agency determined that the Complainant was not qualified to perform the essential functions of the unmodified Mail Handler position, either with or without reasonable accommodation.

The Agency further reasoned that even if the Complainant were otherwise qualified, she failed to submit the requested medical documentation necessary for management to develop an appropriate modified assignment within her medical limitations.

Additionally, the Agency found that the Complainant had not established discrimination under a disparate treatment theory, noting specifically that she had not identified any comparable employees who received differential treatment.
The Complainant subsequently appealed the Agency's decision.

# INVESTIGATION CASE FILE RECORD
## Complainant Background and Claims
The complainant was employed as a Rural Carrier at the Agency's Acton Station in Granbury, Texas.
The complainant filed a formal complaint containing three primary allegations against the Agency.
## Statement of Claims

**Claim 1 and 2 – Compensation Disputes:** Beginning January 5, 2018, and continuing to the present, the complainant alleged that she had not received correct payment for work performed on her assigned route following a route count and adjustment.
Additionally, from April 25, 2018, forward, the complainant asserted that the Agency failed to compensate her for overtime work performed.
The complainant characterized both claims as discriminatory actions in violation of the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA).
**Claim 3 – Denial of Package Assistance:** On December 14, 2018, the complainant requested package assistance from her supervisor, the Customer Service Supervisor, which was subsequently denied.
The complainant alleged this denial constituted retaliation.
## Investigation Conclusion

Following completion of the investigation, the Agency provided the complainant with a copy of the investigation report and notified her of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) Administrative Judge (AJ).
The complainant exercised this right and requested a hearing.
## Administrative Judgment
The assigned AJ determined sua sponte that the complaint did not warrant a hearing proceeding and issued a Notice of Proposed Summary Judgment.
When the complainant failed to submit an objection within the required timeframe, the AJ issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency.
**Analysis of Claim 1 and 2:** The AJ concluded that the complainant failed to establish a prima facie case under GINA.
The complainant's affidavit contained no allegations related to genetic information as the basis for alleged discrimination.

Additionally, the complainant provided no evidence suggesting that management was motivated by genetic information or utilized genetic information in making employment decisions regarding compensation.
**Analysis of Claim 3:** Regarding the package assistance denial, the AJ found that the Customer Service Supervisor provided legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the denial.

The supervisor documented that the complainant had already received assistance earlier that day and was seeking additional help for only one parcel that had subsequently been removed from her delivery route.

The supervisor further noted that remaining packages did not meet established assistance criteria, including considerations regarding vehicle capacity, time constraints, and daily volume requirements.
The AJ determined the complainant failed to demonstrate that these stated reasons constituted pretext for retaliation.
## Final Order
The Agency issued a final order fully implementing the AJ's findings.
The AJ determined that the complainant failed to prove the Agency engaged in discrimination as alleged.
