# INVESTIGATION CASE FILE REPORT
## CASE SUMMARY AND BACKGROUND

This case involves an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint filed by a former employee of the Department of Veterans Affairs, East Orange Veterans Affairs Medical Center, located in East Orange, New Jersey.
At the time of the events that gave rise to this complaint, the Complainant held the position of Primary Care Physician at the Grade Level GS-15.
The Complainant's employment relationship with the Agency culminated in her termination on January 22, 2021, following a recommendation from the Agency's Professional Standards Board.
The Complainant filed her EEO complaint on August 2, 2021, challenging her termination and seeking relief based on allegations of employment discrimination.
Subsequently, the Agency issued its final decision finding no discrimination, which the Complainant then appealed to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.
This matter remains pending before the Commission.
## EMPLOYMENT POSITION AND ESSENTIAL DUTIES
The Complainant was appointed to her position as a Primary Care Physician at the East Orange Veterans Affairs Medical Center on March 3, 2019, subject to completion of a two-year probationary period.
In her capacity as a Primary Care Physician, the Complainant's position entailed several essential job functions and responsibilities.
These duties required her to conduct daily patient interviews and examinations, typically involving approximately twelve patients per day.
Her clinical responsibilities encompassed both in-person, face-to-face patient visits and virtual patient consultations.
Additionally, the Complainant was responsible for documenting all patient visits within the Agency's electronic medical record system, which required proficiency in computer usage and data entry.

As part of her comprehensive patient care responsibilities, the Complainant was also required to order consultations, laboratory tests, and medications using the Agency's electronic medical record system.
The performance of these duties was essential to the position and constituted the core responsibilities of a Primary Care Physician at the facility.
## MEDICAL CONDITIONS AND ACCOMMODATION REQUESTS
The Complainant's medical history relevant to this case began on July 12, 2019, when she sustained an initial injury to her shoulder.
However, the record indicates that the Complainant did not immediately notify her supervisors of this injury or request reasonable accommodation at that time.
Subsequently, in December 2019, the Complainant aggravated a prior injury to her right shoulder and notified her supervisors of this additional injury shortly after its occurrence.

The Complainant attributed multiple functional limitations to her physical condition, including an inability to lift her right arm, inability to operate a computer mouse or keyboard, inability to write, and general limitations in fine motor manipulation of her right hand.

As a result of these claimed limitations, the Complainant asserted that she was unable to perform necessary physical examinations on patients, unable to document clinical notes in the electronic medical record system, and unable to use a computer for extended periods.
The Complainant's immediate supervisor, hereinafter referred to as S1, became aware of the Complainant's right shoulder condition in December 2019.
On February 25, 2020, the Complainant made an initial verbal request for reasonable accommodation and subsequently submitted a formal request under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA).

This formal accommodation request specified several modifications to her work duties, including no lifting restrictions, prohibition on prolonged upper extremity fine manipulation with the right arm and hand, reduction to part-time status with a maximum of twenty hours per week, restrictions on grabbing or grasping activities, and provision of assistance with computer-related tasks as needed.
## INTERACTIVE PROCESS AND ACCOMMODATION ATTEMPTS
Following her return to work on March 2, 2020, after a period of leave beginning in December 2019, the Complainant was granted work shift restrictions as she had requested.
These restrictions permitted her to work four hours per day while taking four hours of Leave Without Pay (LWOP), continuing this schedule for five days per week.

Upon her return to work, the Complainant was required to complete mandatory online training modules through the Agency's Talent Management System and to see between two and three patients by the end of that first week if operationally necessary.
The Complainant, however, failed to see any patients during this initial return period and did not complete the required training modules.

A Medical Assistant employed at the facility documented that on March 4, 2020, the Complainant declined to see a patient who was already waiting in the clinic and who had been on the scheduling list for several months.

When questioned about her refusal, the Complainant indicated that she could not see the patient due to her shoulder condition and stated that her shoulder was bothering her considerably, to the extent that she could barely hold a pen to write clinical notes.

On March 5, 2020, the Complainant's immediate supervisor, her second-level supervisor (hereinafter referred to as S2), and the Agency's Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator held a formal meeting to initiate the interactive process regarding the Complainant's accommodation request.

During this meeting, the Complainant explicitly stated that she could not perform physical patient examinations, was unable to complete necessary patient paperwork, and was unable to utilize a computer for more than a few minutes at any given time.

Given the Agency's concern that even part-time in-person work might exacerbate her medical condition, the Agency decided to grant the Complainant an alternative accommodation consisting of continued LWOP status to allow for rehabilitation of her injury over a specified six-week period.
The Complainant remained in an approved LWOP status from March 4, 2020, through August 10, 2020.
Approximately two weeks following the March 5 meeting, the Complainant submitted a request for one hundred percent telework accommodations.

In response, on March 25, 2020, S1 requested that the Complainant provide physician documentation addressing her ability to perform the essential functions of her position, specifically including documentation of her limitations with typing notes, placing orders and consults, sending laboratory letters, and completing paperwork and forms required for patient care.

During this period, the Agency was simultaneously responding to the COVID-19 pandemic, during which non-urgent medical appointments were cancelled, and telework arrangements for hospital physicians were implemented on an ad hoc basis, typically involving fifty percent telework with alternating weeks of in-person hospital work and remote teleworking from home.
Concurrently, the Agency made substantial efforts to accommodate the Complainant's needs through various technological and ergonomic modifications.

These accommodations included preparation and installation of dictation software on the Complainant's computer to minimize the necessity for typing; procurement and delivery of two ergonomic chairs, one for each of her examination rooms; shipment of ergonomic mice and keyboards to both her home and office locations; and approval for issuance of a laptop computer on March 3, 2020, though delivery was delayed due to equipment shortages related to the pandemic.

S1 subsequently submitted a second laptop request through the Computer and Electronic Accommodation (CAP) program, which operates within the Department of Defense, in an effort to expedite equipment delivery.

However, the CAP program denied this request, citing insufficient medical documentation submitted during the Needs Assessment to support the necessity for a second laptop, as well as the absence of a signed telework agreement.

On June 2, 2020, the Agency eventually secured a laptop for the Complainant; however, the Complainant never executed the required telework agreement, which would have addressed her teleworking arrangement for a temporary period of one to three months in light of her temporary disability status.

S1 indicated that the Agency could not accommodate the Complainant's request for unconditional one hundred percent telework for an extended period of at least one year because the Complainant had failed to provide adequate medical documentation to justify such an extended accommodation.

Furthermore, S1 noted that the hospital was experiencing a significant shortage of physicians, that certain providers were absent due to illness from COVID-19, and that the Complainant's patient caseload was being managed by other physicians during her absence.

Based on these considerations, the Agency offered the Complainant a telework agreement for a temporary period of one to three months, with the duration to be determined based on updates to her medical documentation and reassessment by her treating physician.
The Complainant declined to accept the Agency's offered telework agreement.
## MEDICAL DOCUMENTATION AND ACCOMMODATION COORDINATOR ACTIONS
The Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator documented that the Complainant made several separate accommodation requests, including a formal request on April 21, 2020.

In that request, the Complainant sought one hundred percent telework, a reduction to twenty hours per work week, and modified work assignments to be implemented either for a one-year period or on a permanent basis.

The Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator stated, and the record confirms, that she made numerous requests of the Complainant, including several written emails in June 2020, requesting provision of medical documentation to support the Complainant's reasonable accommodation requests and to establish the existence and nature of her claimed disability.

The Coordinator specifically requested that the Complainant provide medical documentation demonstrating the effectiveness of telework and telemedicine accommodations in relation to her medical condition, as well as information establishing the expected duration of her medical condition, including whether her condition was temporary or permanent in nature.

The Coordinator also requested that the Complainant provide authorization and consent for the Agency to contact her treating physician in order to gather necessary information and proceed with processing her accommodation request.
Despite these repeated and documented requests, the Complainant failed to provide the requested medical documentation or authorization.

Consequently, on August 7, 2020, the Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator closed the Complainant's reasonable accommodation request file and formally notified the Complainant that the case would be reopened if she subsequently provided the requested documentation.
## MEDICAL RECORDS ANALYSIS
The record reflects that the Complainant provided the Agency with copies of Return to Work statements from her treating physicians.

In a Return to Work statement dated January 13, 2020, the Complainant's first treating physician, hereinafter referred to as DR1, documented that the Complainant had been seen in his office on that date and could return to work after a follow-up examination scheduled for February 10, 2020.
In a subsequent Return to Work statement dated February 10, 2020, DR1 documented that the Complainant had been examined on that date and was medically cleared to return to work on March 2, 2020.
Additionally, the record contains a medical statement from a second treating physician, hereinafter referred to as DR2, dated February 25, 2020.

In that statement, DR2 documented that the Complainant was under his care for her right shoulder condition and recommended that she be assigned light duty and part-time work with restrictions on lifting.
DR2 further recommended that the Complainant be provided assistance with computer-related tasks and stated that her status and readiness to return to full duty would be reevaluated in six weeks.

In a subsequent statement dated April 21, 2020, DR2 recommended that the Complainant be allowed to continue on light duty status, work from home utilizing a laptop computer, and provide telemedicine services to patients.
DR2 indicated that the Complainant's status for return to full duty would be reevaluated on May 19, 2020.
In two separate medical statements, both dated May 19, 2020, DR2 documented that the Complainant had been evaluated on that date for her right shoulder condition.
The physician noted that the Complainant continued to experience dexterity issues and recommended that she continue physical therapy to address shoulder exercises and functional limitations.

DR2 stated that the Complainant was able to use a computer and mouse with appropriate ergonomic support and indicated that her status for return to normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks.
On July 15, 2020, the Complainant submitted a statement from DR2 dated June 22, 2020.
In this statement, DR2 recommended that the Complainant be allowed to work from home via telemedicine services, with a maximum of twenty hours per week.

The physician documented that the Complainant continued to experience pain with associated dexterity issues, including difficulties with gripping and right arm and hand manipulation, and reported pain and functional difficulties when performing activities such as gripping the steering wheel while driving.
DR2 recommended continuation of physical therapy and noted that the Complainant was able to use a computer and mouse with ergonomic support.
The physician indicated that the Complainant's status for return to normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks.
In a final statement dated July 30, 2020, DR2 reiterated the foregoing clinical findings and recommendations.

Additionally, DR2 noted that he was recommending evaluation by a spine specialist for the Complainant's condition, stated that her return to work status would be reevaluated, and documented that the Complainant's "shoulder symptoms are well controlled and is discharged at this time" from his direct care.
## AWOL DETERMINATION AND TERMINATION

Following the closure of the Complainant's reasonable accommodation case by the Coordinator, S1 and S2 indicated that the Coordinator suggested it would be appropriate and reasonable to place the Complainant in Absent Without Leave (AWOL) status for her continued absence from work.

Management considered the Coordinator's recommendation in conjunction with the fact that the Complainant had not reported for work for nearly eight months and had not provided the medical documentation that the Agency had repeatedly requested.
Based on these factors, management determined that it was appropriate to place the Complainant in AWOL status beginning August 10, 2020.
The Agency documented that the Complainant had utilized all available annual leave and sick leave accruals during the period from December 20, 2019, through February 6, 2020.

Subsequently, the Complainant was granted LWOP in increments as follows: eighty hours for February 7 through February 29, 2020; four hundred eighty hours for March 2 through March 26, 2020; and four hundred twenty-one hours for March 26 through August 7, 2020.
The Complainant remained in AWOL status from August 10, 2020, until her subsequent termination on January 22, 2021.
## ADMINISTRATIVE JUDGE DECISION

The Administrative Judge (AJ) issued a decision finding no discrimination, concluding that the Complainant failed to establish that the Agency had wrongfully denied her request for reasonable accommodation.

The AJ determined that the Complainant had failed to provide adequate medical documentation demonstrating her ability to perform the essential functions of her position, specifically her ability to perform physical examinations of patients.

The AJ found that although the Complainant alleged she suffered from limitations in using her right arm, she had provided limited documentation to support the existence of a disability as defined under applicable law.
The AJ noted that all medical documentation provided indicated that her treating physician would conduct reassessments at future dates.

Despite the Agency's repeated requests, the Complainant failed to provide any medical documentation establishing a formal diagnosis of her condition or its duration—specifically, whether her condition was temporary or permanent in nature.

The AJ further found that the Complainant had failed to execute a release authorization permitting the Agency to obtain medical information from her treating physicians and had declined to provide even the investigator with a release authorizing disclosure of her medical information.

The AJ additionally found that the Complainant had not demonstrated that she would be able to work from home through telework, as the Complainant herself had admitted that she was unable to use a pen or computer without assistance.

The AJ noted that the permanent accommodation the Complainant was requesting—telework—was one for which she was not qualified, as telework would require an increase in computer usage, and as a Primary Care Physician, the Complainant was required to perform physical examinations of patients even in a telework arrangement.

The AJ found that the Complainant had stated she was unable to perform such physical examinations on March 4, 2020, and had never subsequently provided documentation demonstrating that she had regained the ability to perform this essential function.

The AJ concluded that the Complainant had refused to engage with the Agency regarding these critical issues by failing to provide the requested medical documentation, thereby causing the Agency to close her accommodation case without issuing either a formal denial or approval of her request.
## APPEAL AND PENDING MATTER
The Agency did not issue a separate final order, and the Administrative Judge's decision effectively became the final action of the Agency.
The Complainant has appealed from this final action, contesting the Agency's finding of no discrimination.

# CASE FILE MEMORANDUM: INVESTIGATION RECORD
## CASE SUMMARY AND BACKGROUND
This memorandum documents the formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint filed by the Complainant, a highly educated research scientist employed by the Agency's National Institute on Aging.
During the relevant period, the Complainant worked as a Biologist at the GS-0401-11 level until her promotion to GS-12 in May 2013.
She was assigned to the Laboratory of Neurogenetics, specifically within the Neuromuscular Disease Research Section, located in Bethesda, Maryland.
On November 8, 2017, the Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint, which was subsequently amended to include additional allegations of discrimination and hostile work environment conditions.
## PROTECTED CLASS CHARACTERISTICS AND BASES FOR COMPLAINT
The Complainant identifies herself as belonging to multiple protected classes under federal employment discrimination law.
She alleges discrimination based on the following characteristics: race and color (specifically, African American/Black descent), national origin (Guyanese nationality), and sex (female).

Additionally, the Complainant reported several disability conditions that form a basis for her claims, including a diagnosis of bipolar disorder in 2009, which was later re-diagnosed as Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in 2017, generalized anxiety disorder, benign mitral valve prolapse, and fibroid tumors requiring surgical intervention in December 2013.
The Complainant also asserts claims of reprisal based on her initiation of EEO counseling proceedings on July 27, 2017, relating to the instant complaint.
## SUPERVISORY RELATIONSHIPS AND KEY PERSONNEL
The Complainant's direct supervisor during the period at issue was the Section Chief, identified as Ireland, a Caucasian male.

The Section Chief served as the Complainant's first-line supervisor and maintained responsibility for assigning work, conducting performance-related communications, and overseeing the day-to-day operations of the Section.
The Complainant's second-line supervisor was the Lab Chief, identified as British and Caucasian, to whom she was reassigned in February 2018 following the initiation of her EEO complaint.
## SPECIFIC INCIDENTS AND ALLEGATIONS
The Complainant's amended complaint encompasses numerous specific incidents spanning from 2009 through April 2018.
In June 2017, the Section Chief failed to conduct a scheduled meeting with the Complainant.

Shortly thereafter, on June 15, 2017, the Section Chief notified the Complainant of a reassignment to DNA plate preparation duties, a role typically assigned to summer interns and student employees rather than doctoral-level biologists.
Following the Complainant's initiation of EEO counseling on July 27, 2017, the record reflects several alleged retaliatory actions.
Agency management excluded the Complainant from a major project within her laboratory.
The Section Chief reportedly ceased communicating with her regarding work assignments, and management failed to assign her additional projects.
On February 23, 2018, the Section Chief did not promote the Complainant as allegedly promised.
The allegations of hostile work environment span nearly a decade.
According to the Complainant, beginning in 2009, the Section Chief subjected her to inappropriate comments and unfair treatment.

In 2009, he directed laboratory employees to engage in a project, made inappropriate comments, then retracted those comments while joking that he should refrain from further remarks lest an EEO complaint be filed against him.
In 2010, the Section Chief allegedly stated that the Agency would submit research findings to a top-tier journal without the Complainant's authorship because the work required perfection.
During the same year, he purportedly called the Complainant an "idiot" while deliberately distracting her during an experimental procedure and required her to work on Christmas Day.
He repeatedly criticized her writing speed and the duration of her doctoral program completion.

In March 2011, after the Complainant was assigned to lead a task force, she experienced difficulties because the Section Chief frequently excluded her from electronic communications concerning task assignments.
In April 2011, he made a statement suggesting that no one would tolerate her mental illness outside the current employment relationship.
In September 2011, following her meeting with Career Services, the Section Chief questioned her decision to seek career guidance and suggested she remain in her current position.
Approximately during the same period, the Complainant alleges the Section Chief placed her name last on a research article.
In 2011, he made a comment suggesting she would enjoy the film "The Help." In 2012, he made jokes regarding her African ancestry.
By 2013, he had engaged in uncomfortable exchanges concerning her family background and ancestry.

Additional allegations from 2013 include the Section Chief directing post-baccalaureate students to review the Complainant's work, referring to her as a "Diva" in a manner that discouraged colleague interaction, and precluding her from authoring manuscripts for top-tier journals.
From 2016 onward, the Section Chief failed to attend their regularly scheduled one-on-one meetings and warned the Complainant not to knock on his closed office door.
In May 2017, after initially indicating he would include her, the Section Chief excluded the Complainant from a project.
On May 12, 2017, he yelled at her before colleagues, stating "No wonder nothing you do ever works" in response to her answer regarding laboratory protocols.
## MEDICAL PRIVACY VIOLATION AND DISABILITY DISCRIMINATION
In 2013, the Section Chief disclosed to a colleague that the Complainant had a heart condition and expressed dissatisfaction regarding the management of her medical issues.

The Complainant denies ever disclosing her heart condition to either the Section Chief or the Lab Chief, asserting the Section Chief made this statement to preemptively protect himself from potential accusations of disclosing confidential medical information.
The Complainant underwent surgical removal of fibroid tumors on December 18, 2013, requiring hospitalization and six weeks of recovery.
Additionally, in late May or early June 2017, the Section Chief reportedly laughed with a colleague and trainee about an incident requiring the Complainant to work on Christmas Day.
## RESOURCE ALLOCATION AND EQUIPMENT DISCRIMINATION
The Complainant alleges that in June 2015, the Section Chief required her to accept a lower-specification computer compared to other laboratory employees.

Additionally, the Section Chief acknowledged the Complainant deserved a promotion in 2015 but deliberately delayed processing the promotion paperwork until 2017, coinciding with an announced hiring freeze.
The Complainant was notified of the indefinite hiring freeze in February 2017.
## POST-COMPLAINT RETALIATION AND EXCLUSION
Following the initiation of EEO counseling, the record reflects additional concerning actions.
In February 2018, the Agency reassigned the Complainant to report directly to the Lab Chief, ostensibly due to her EEO complaint.

In March 2018, the Lab Chief repositioned the Complainant's photograph in the breakroom under a different laboratory group, despite her continued membership in the Neuromuscular Disease Research Section.
In March 2018, the Section Chief failed to communicate directly with the Complainant regarding an ongoing collaborative project, preventing her participation.

# CASE FILE MEMORANDUM: INVESTIGATION RECORD
## CASE SUMMARY AND BACKGROUND
This memorandum documents the formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint filed by the Complainant, a highly educated research scientist employed by the Agency's National Institute on Aging.

She was assigned to the Laboratory of Neurogenetics, specifically within the Neuromuscular Disease Research Section, located in Bethesda, Maryland.
On November 9, 2017, the Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint, which was subsequently amended to include additional allegations of discrimination and hostile work environment conditions.
## PROTECTED CLASS CHARACTERISTICS AND BASES FOR COMPLAINT
The Complainant identifies herself as belonging to multiple protected classes under federal employment discrimination law.
She alleges discrimination based on the following characteristics: race and color (specifically, African American/Black descent), national origin (Guyanese nationality), and sex (female).

Additionally, the Complainant reported several disability conditions that form a basis for her claims, including a diagnosis of bipolar disorder in 2009, which was later re-diagnosed as Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in 2017, generalized anxiety disorder, benign mitral valve prolapse, and fibroid tumors requiring surgical intervention in December 2013.
The Complainant also asserts claims of reprisal based on her initiation of EEO counseling proceedings on July 27, 2017, relating to the instant complaint.
## SUPERVISORY RELATIONSHIPS AND KEY PERSONNEL
The Complainant's direct supervisor during the period at issue was the Section Chief, identified as Ireland, a Caucasian male.

The Section Chief served as the Complainant's first-line supervisor and maintained responsibility for assigning work, conducting performance-related communications, and overseeing the day-to-day operations of the Section.
The Complainant's second-line supervisor was the Lab Chief, identified as British and Caucasian, to whom she was reassigned in February 2018 following the initiation of her EEO complaint.

The Complainant's amended complaint encompasses numerous specific incidents spanning from 2009 through April 2018.
In June 2017, the Section Chief failed to conduct a scheduled meeting with the Complainant.

Shortly thereafter, on June 15, 2017, the Section Chief notified the Complainant of a reassignment to DNA plate preparation duties, a role typically assigned to summer interns and student employees rather than doctoral-level biologists.
Following the Complainant's initiation of EEO counseling on July 27, 2017, the record reflects several alleged retaliatory actions.
Agency management excluded the Complainant from a major project within her laboratory.
The Section Chief reportedly ceased communicating with her regarding work assignments, and management failed to assign her additional projects.
On February 23, 2018, the Section Chief did not promote the Complainant as allegedly promised.
The allegations of hostile work environment span nearly a decade.
According to the Complainant, beginning in 2009, the Section Chief subjected her to inappropriate comments and unfair treatment.

In 2010, the Section Chief allegedly stated that the Agency would submit research findings to a top-tier journal without the Complainant's authorship because the work required perfection.

He repeatedly criticized her writing speed and the duration of her doctoral program completion.

In March 2011, after the Complainant was assigned to lead a task force, she experienced difficulties because the Section Chief frequently excluded her from electronic communications concerning task assignments.
In April 2011, he made a statement suggesting that no one would tolerate her mental illness outside the current employment relationship.
In September 2011, following her meeting with Career Services, the Section Chief questioned her decision to seek career guidance and suggested she remain in her current position.
Approximately during the same period, the Complainant alleges the Section Chief placed her name last on a research article.
In 2011, he made a comment suggesting she would enjoy the film "The Help." In 2012, he made jokes regarding her African ancestry.
By 2013, he had engaged in uncomfortable exchanges concerning her family background and ancestry.

Additional allegations from 2013 include the Section Chief directing post-baccalaureate students to review the Complainant's work, referring to her as a "Diva" in a manner that discouraged colleague interaction, and precluding her from authoring manuscripts for top-tier journals.
From 2016 onward, the Section Chief failed to attend their regularly scheduled one-on-one meetings and warned the Complainant not to knock on his closed office door.
In May 2017, after initially indicating he would include her, the Section Chief excluded the Complainant from a project.
On May 12, 2017, he yelled at her before colleagues, stating "No wonder nothing you do ever works" in response to her answer regarding laboratory protocols.
## MEDICAL PRIVACY VIOLATION AND DISABILITY DISCRIMINATION
In 2013, the Section Chief disclosed to a colleague that the Complainant had a heart condition and expressed dissatisfaction regarding the management of her medical issues.

The Complainant denies ever disclosing her heart condition to either the Section Chief or the Lab Chief, asserting the Section Chief made this statement to preemptively protect himself from potential accusations of disclosing confidential medical information.
The Complainant underwent surgical removal of fibroid tumors on December 18, 2013, requiring hospitalization and six weeks of recovery.
Additionally, in late May or early June 2017, the Section Chief reportedly laughed with a colleague and trainee about an incident requiring the Complainant to work on Christmas Day.
## RESOURCE ALLOCATION AND EQUIPMENT DISCRIMINATION
The Complainant alleges that in June 2015, the Section Chief required her to accept a lower-specification computer compared to other laboratory employees.

Additionally, the Section Chief acknowledged the Complainant deserved a promotion in 2015 but deliberately delayed processing the promotion paperwork until 2017, coinciding with an announced hiring freeze.
The Complainant was notified of the indefinite hiring freeze in February 2017.

In February 2018, the Agency reassigned the Complainant to report directly to the Lab Chief, ostensibly due to her EEO complaint.

In March 2018, the Lab Chief repositioned the Complainant's photograph in the breakroom under a different laboratory group, despite her continued membership in the Neuromuscular Disease Research Section.
In March 2018, the Section Chief failed to communicate directly with the Complainant regarding an ongoing collaborative project, preventing her participation.
On April 5, 2018, the Section Chief publicly announced to staff that the Complainant no longer reported to him.

Subsequently, in April 2018, the Agency removed the Complainant's name from the National Institute on Aging website staff listing—a significant action given that her position required interaction with external agencies and collaborators.
Finally, on April 23, 2018, all employees and collaborators began copying the Lab Chief on every email sent to the Complainant, regardless of the message's significance.

Following an Administrative Judge's remand for final decision, the Agency dismissed claims six through eleven for failure to timely initiate EEO counseling.
The Agency found no discrimination on the remaining claims.
On appeal, the Complainant documented that more than fifteen months elapsed after the Administrative Judge's prescribed sixty-day period without issuance of a Final Agency Decision.
The Complainant submitted evidence that on May 20, 2020, she inquired about the status of the decision.
She argues this extraordinary delay warrants a default judgment sanction against the Agency.
The Agency did not submit a reply to the appeal.
# INVESTIGATION RECORD - CASE FILE DOCUMENTATION
## Case Overview and Background
This investigation record documents an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) discrimination complaint filed against the Agency by a former employee.

At the time of the events in question, the Complainant was employed as a probationary Credentials Assistant at the Agency's Naval Medical Center in Portsmouth, Virginia, at the GS-0303-07 grade level.
Her employment was terminated on August 2, 2018.

On November 8, 2018, approximately three months following her termination, the Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency had discriminated against her based on her race, specifically identifying herself as African-American.

Following the completion of the formal investigation, the Complainant was provided with a copy of the investigation report along with written notification of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge.
The Complainant exercised this right and requested a hearing.
## Hearing Proceedings and Direct Evidence Claims
During the hearing conducted by the Administrative Judge (AJ), the Complainant presented testimony along with documentary evidence in support of her discrimination claim.
The Complainant's primary allegation centered on the conduct of her second-level supervisor, identified as the Department Head at grade GS-0301-12.
The Complainant testified that this supervisor made the decision to terminate her employment upon learning that the Complainant's significant other was White.

The Complainant further testified that the supervisor became aware of this interracial relationship in May 2018 and that the supervisor's demeanor and treatment of her changed noticeably following this discovery.

Additionally, the Complainant testified that her first-level supervisor, the Professional Affairs Coordinator serving as Assistant Department Head at grade GS-0301-11, had specifically warned her not to permit the second-level supervisor to learn about her relationship with a White man.
This first-level supervisor's alleged warning was presented as evidence that both supervisors were aware of a discriminatory prejudice within the management structure.
## Witness Testimony and Corroboration Attempts
To support her theory that the second-level supervisor discriminated against her based on race, the Complainant presented a key witness—a coworker employed as a Program Analyst at grade GS-0303-07.
This coworker testified that the second-level supervisor had made open statements concerning her husband's extreme bias against interracial relationships.

The coworker also testified that the second-level supervisor had expressed surprise at the Complainant's dating relationship with a White man and claimed to have heard the supervisor make additional race-related remarks on various occasions.
Both the Complainant and the coworker testified that the first-level supervisor had previously warned them about the second-level supervisor's documented prejudicial attitudes.
## Credibility Determinations and Analysis
The Administrative Judge found the testimony regarding the interracial relationship theory to be lacking in credibility.

The AJ identified what it characterized as a "glaring omission" of any reference to the interracial relationship theory in the Complainant's original EEO complaint, in the EEO counseling records, or in the Complainant's affidavit submitted during the investigation phase.

The AJ reasoned that evidence of this nature, if genuinely credible and material to the Complainant's claim, would have been raised immediately rather than appearing for the first time approximately three years after the termination occurred.
During the EEO counseling process and in her formal affidavit, the Complainant had articulated different theories regarding why her termination occurred.

She indicated that she believed the termination resulted from events that took place during a work conference held in Leesburg, Virginia, where the second-level supervisor allegedly engaged in inappropriate conduct.
The Complainant had theorized that the supervisor terminated her because the supervisor feared the Complainant would disclose information about these inappropriate incidents.

Additionally, the Complainant had suggested that her termination was connected to the second-level supervisor's mistaken belief that the Complainant had filed a formal grievance against her, when in fact the grievance had been filed by a different employee.
The AJ noted that these previously articulated theories bore no apparent connection to racial discrimination.

When questioned by Agency counsel during cross-examination about her failure to raise the interracial relationship theory previously, the Complainant provided no explanation for the significant omission.

Similarly, the AJ found that any reference to the second-level supervisor's alleged prejudice against interracial couples was "conspicuously missing" from the coworker's affidavit that had been submitted during the investigation.

The coworker's affidavit had referenced the Leesburg training events and stated a belief that the Complainant had been discriminated against because she was African-American with greater experience than management.

The coworker had also stated that the first-level supervisor had made racially inappropriate remarks but had made no mention whatsoever of the Complainant's partner being White or the second-level supervisor's opposition to such relationships.
When the first-level supervisor testified at the hearing, she denied having made any comments characterizing the second-level supervisor as racist.
## Legitimate Nondiscriminatory Reason for Termination
The Agency articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for the Complainant's termination as documented in the formal Notice of Termination.
The Agency stated that the termination resulted from the Complainant's failure to properly follow the established privileging and credentialing process.

Specifically, the Agency alleged that the Complainant had misrepresented to her leadership that a healthcare provider had specifically requested certain privileges when, in fact, the Complainant herself had made the request to the provider.
According to the provider's account, the Complainant had attempted to convince him to apply for privileges that he had not previously sought.
The incident in question involved a credentialing and privileges application processed by the Complainant.
The provider had selected incorrect privileges based upon the Complainant's mistaken understanding of the proper protocol for credentialing contract providers.
The Complainant acknowledged that her guidance to the provider was inaccurate at the time it was provided.

This erroneous guidance resulted in a significant delay to the provider's application and prevented him from receiving the proper credentials necessary to practice within the Agency until his existing privileges were scheduled to expire.

The provider subsequently contacted the Complainant's supervisors to express frustration regarding the application delay, attributing the problem to the incorrect guidance the Complainant had provided.
## Credibility of the Termination Basis

The Administrative Judge found the provider credible when he testified that he and the Complainant had discussed the privileges application prior to his submission of it and that he had submitted the application based upon the Complainant's instructions.
Conversely, the AJ found the Complainant "not credible" in her testimony that she had never communicated with the provider before he submitted the initial application.

The AJ concluded that the Complainant had failed to prove pretext because no evidence demonstrated that any similarly situated employee had been involved in a similar episode or had acted dishonestly with managers without being terminated.
The Notice of Termination also cited that the Complainant had failed to initiate the renewal privileging and credentialing process within the required ninety-day timeframe.
The AJ found this allegation to be factually inaccurate.
The AJ identified a similarly situated employee who had multiple renewals nearing expiration with fewer than ninety days remaining but had not been terminated.

However, the AJ found that because this reason alone would not have supported termination, and because the primary reason for termination was the misrepresentation regarding the provider's privileges request, the presence of this secondary reason did not undermine the Agency's stated justification.
## Final Determination
The Administrative Judge issued a decision finding in favor of the Agency.
The AJ determined that the Complainant had failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

When the Agency failed to issue a final order within the required forty-day period following receipt of the AJ's decision, the AJ's decision became the Agency's final action pursuant to federal regulations.
The Complainant subsequently appealed this decision.

# INVESTIGATIVE CASE FILE REPORT
## COMPLAINANT INFORMATION AND EMPLOYMENT BACKGROUND

At the time of the events giving rise to this complaint, the Complainant was employed as a Travel Specialist, classified at the GS-6 grade level, within the Agency's Office of Infectious Disease (OID).
This office operates under the broader organizational structure of the National Center for HIV/AIDS, Viral Hepatitis, STD and TB Prevention (NCHHSTP), located in Atlanta, Georgia.
The Complainant's employment file and position responsibilities are documented in the Report of Investigation (ROI) at page 49.
During the relevant timeframe, the Complainant reported to multiple supervisory authorities.
Her first-level supervisor (S1) held the position of Supervisor Program Specialist, classified at the GS-12 grade level.
The S1 supervisor is an African American female.
Additionally, the Complainant was supervised by a Management Officer, identified as a Caucasian male, and a Deputy Director, identified as a male of unspecified racial or ethnic background.
These overlapping supervisory relationships would prove significant in the development of the allegations that follow.
## ALLEGED HOSTILE WORK ENVIRONMENT AND SUPERVISORY MISCONDUCT
### Incident of October 28, 2013
According to the Complainant's account, on October 28, 2013, during a workplace meeting, the S1 supervisor made several derogatory and threatening statements.
Specifically, the Complainant alleges that S1 instructed her to leave the Agency, stating that upper management did not favor her.
The Complainant further contends that S1 indicated the Management Officer was deliberately working against her interests.
Most significantly, the Complainant claims that S1 directed her to withdraw her union membership, using profane language and asserting that union affiliation would prevent career advancement.
This account is documented in the ROI at page 127.
However, the S1 supervisor categorically denied making these statements.
The S1 supervisor further denied that any such meeting or incident transpired.
The denial places this matter in direct contradiction, with no corroborating witnesses identified to support either account.
### Christmas Party Incident
The Complainant also reported an interaction with the Business Services Support Specialist regarding her absence from the office Christmas party.
According to the Complainant's testimony, the Support Specialist questioned why she was not attending the event and inquired whether she celebrated Christmas.
The Complainant explained that she practices the Jehovah's Witness faith and therefore does not participate in Christmas celebrations.
This testimony appears in the ROI at pages 129-30.
The Complainant describes the Support Specialist's non-verbal response as particularly offensive.

The Complainant asserts that the Support Specialist's facial expression conveyed disgust, characterized as looking at her "as if she had a disease," and that the Support Specialist rolled her eyes in response to this religious disclosure.
The Complainant experienced this reaction as dismissive and disrespectful of her religious beliefs.

However, the Support Specialist provided a contrary account, stating she had no recollection of any interaction with the Complainant on the referenced date and maintaining that the incident, as described by the Complainant, never occurred.
### Alleged Coworker Comments of January 9, 2014
The Complainant further alleged that on January 9, 2014, she overheard a conversation between two coworkers—identified as C1 and C2—in which disparaging comments were made about her.

According to the Complainant, C1 remarked to C2 that the Complainant thinks "she is cute because she is built like a Black girl" and characterized the Complainant as "bad news and not your friend." The Complainant reported that such comments were repeated on multiple occasions, occurring in hallways and in the office elevator.
These allegations are documented in the ROI at pages 131-32.
The Complainant's account stands in stark contrast to the denials offered by both coworkers.
Coworker C1 maintained that she had no knowledge of the Complainant's identity and categorically denied making any such comments.
Coworker C2 similarly asserted that she did not recall C1 making such a comment to her.
Without corroborating evidence or witness testimony, this matter remains unresolved through contradictory accounts.
## ALLEGATIONS OF SEXUAL HARASSMENT BY THE DEPUTY DIRECTOR

The Complainant raised the most serious allegations against the Deputy Director, describing a pattern of unwanted sexual conduct spanning multiple years, with origins in 2006 and continuing through the investigation period.
These allegations encompass physical contact, verbal advances, and alleged retaliatory employment actions.
### Physical Contact Allegations
The Complainant testified that the Deputy Director engaged in inappropriate physical conduct during official workplace settings.
Specifically, the Complainant alleged that the Deputy Director would frequently stare at her chest.
Additionally, the Complainant claimed that on two separate occasions during staff meetings, the Deputy Director placed his hand on her left leg and, in her words, "rolled his hand down" her leg.
These incidents are detailed in the ROI at pages 133-35.
The Complainant described her response to the first instance of physical contact, stating that she "scooted over" to create distance between herself and the Deputy Director.
However, when this conduct repeated at a second staff meeting, the Complainant reported that she left the meeting prematurely.

The Complainant further stated that she verbally communicated her discomfort to the Deputy Director, informing him that his physical contact with her leg during meetings was causing her emotional distress and was unwelcome.

Beyond the leg contact during meetings, the Complainant also alleged that the Deputy Director regularly entered her work cubicle and placed his hands on her shoulders, engaging in what appeared to be shoulder massage motions.

The Complainant further contended that the Deputy Director would lean in close proximity to her while directing her attention to her computer monitor, thereby invading her personal space in a manner she found uncomfortable and inappropriate.
### Unwanted Social Advances
The Complainant reported that the Deputy Director extended social invitations to her, specifically requesting lunch and/or dinner engagements.
The Complainant consistently rejected these advances, refusing to accept the Deputy Director's social invitations.
### Alleged Retaliatory Actions Following Rejection of Advances
The Complainant maintained that following her rejection of the Deputy Director's social overtures, he engaged in retaliatory workplace conduct designed to punish her refusal.
The Complainant outlined several specific forms of alleged retaliation.
First, the Deputy Director allegedly assigned her additional job duties beyond her normal responsibilities.
Second, he purportedly refused to approve her requests for professional training and development opportunities.
Third, he allegedly assigned her duties that fell outside the scope of her position description as a Travel Specialist.

Fourth, the Complainant reported that the Deputy Director engaged in aggressive verbal conduct, yelling and cursing at her in his office regarding the proper processing of employee travel preparations.
This account is documented in the ROI at page 53.
The Complainant also described volatile behavioral episodes by the Deputy Director.
The Complainant testified that the Deputy Director would summon her to his office and engage in loud, angry venting while throwing objects such as pens and pencils across the room.
According to the Complainant's account, these outbursts occurred with sufficient frequency that coworkers became aware of the pattern.
The Complainant explained that she discussed the Deputy Director's behavioral pattern with several colleagues who had become aware of her distress.
The ROI at page 154 documents these allegations.
### Initial Reporting and Lack of Response
The Complainant indicated that she reported the Deputy Director's harassing conduct to the Agency Director shortly after the behavior commenced.
However, the Director's response was dismissive—the Complainant reported that the Director "shook his head in disbelief" rather than initiating any remedial action.
The Complainant testified that this lack of responsiveness resulted in the harassment continuing unabated.
The ROI at page 134 reflects this account.
The Complainant further maintained that she lodged complaints with her first-level supervisor (S1), the Management Officer, and a Consultant employed by the Agency.
According to the Complainant's account, all three recipients of her complaints failed to take any meaningful action, effectively ignoring her reports of harassment.
However, both the S1 supervisor and the Management Officer denied that the Complainant had ever reported the Deputy Director's conduct to them.
They maintained that they were unaware of any allegations regarding the Deputy Director's harassment of the Complainant.
### Corroborating Witness Testimony
Despite the management denials, multiple coworkers provided testimony corroborating significant elements of the Complainant's allegations.
The Senior Budget Analyst provided detailed testimony that the Complainant would visit her office on an almost weekly basis to express frustration about the Deputy Director's conduct.

The Senior Budget Analyst specifically noted that the Complainant complained about the Deputy Director violating her personal space and making her uncomfortable through social invitations and inappropriate remarks.

The Senior Budget Analyst further testified that she had personally observed the Deputy Director engaging in verbal tantrums and yelling, directing this aggressive conduct at the Complainant as if she were a "soundboard" for his emotional discharge.
The Senior Budget Analyst additionally attested that the Complainant visited her office on several occasions in a state of distress, crying over the Deputy Director's behavior.
This testimony appears in the ROI at page 208.
The Team Lead similarly provided testimony that the Complainant approached him on multiple occasions to discuss the Deputy Director's inappropriate conduct.
The Team Lead specifically recalled that the Complainant described inappropriate physical touching that had occurred during a workplace meeting.
The Team Lead further testified that the Complainant had informed him that she had scheduled a meeting with the Management Officer to address the Deputy Director's conduct.
The Team Lead noted that the Complainant subsequently reported to him that the Management Officer had shown little concern for addressing her harassment allegations.
The Team Lead stated that he expressed his skepticism to the Complainant, noting that her efforts with the Management Officer appeared unlikely to produce any meaningful resolution.
This account is documented in the ROI at page 205.
The Resource Management Team Lead provided additional corroborating testimony, describing herself as having frequently served as a "comforting ear" to the Complainant.
This witness testified that the Complainant repeatedly expressed her extreme discomfort with the Deputy Director's conduct.
The Resource Management Team Lead stated that she had frequently observed the Deputy Director in the Complainant's work cubicle on numerous occasions.

While this witness did not directly observe any explicitly inappropriate physical contact or verbal statements, she noted that she found the Deputy Director's frequent encroachment upon the Complainant's personal space to be unusual and noteworthy.
The ROI at page 223 contains this testimony.
The Public Health Advisor Supervisor testified that the Complainant had mentioned that the Deputy Director had touched her leg and had extended dinner invitations.
Significantly, the Public Health Advisor Supervisor disclosed that she herself had been subjected to harassment by the Deputy Director in the past but had chosen not to file a complaint.

The Public Health Advisor Supervisor explained that she feared being the first woman to come forward against the Deputy Director, particularly given his standing and favorable reputation within the Agency.
This fear-based silence reflects a pattern of witness reluctance that may have enabled the continuation of the Deputy Director's conduct.
The ROI at page 199 documents this testimony.
Additional witnesses, including another Team Lead and two other employees, provided testimony confirming that the Complainant had informed them of the Deputy Director's harassing behavior.

The Complainant testified that the Deputy Director engaged in inappropriate physical conduct during official workplace settings.

The Complainant reported that the Deputy Director extended social invitations to her, specifically requesting lunch and/or dinner engagements.
The Complainant consistently rejected these advances, refusing to accept the Deputy Director's social invitations.

The Complainant maintained that following her rejection of the Deputy Director's social overtures, he engaged in retaliatory workplace conduct designed to punish her refusal.

The Senior Budget Analyst additionally attested that the Complainant visited her office on several occasions in a state of distress, crying over the Deputy Director's behavior.
This testimony appears in the ROI at page 208.
The Team Lead similarly provided testimony that the Complainant approached him on multiple occasions to discuss the Deputy Director's inappropriate conduct.

# CASE FILE INVESTIGATION RECORD
## CASE SUMMARY AND BACKGROUND

This investigation concerns employment discrimination allegations filed by a former Library Director, position classification NF-1410-IV, who was employed at the Agency's Joint Base Andrews facility located in Prince George's County, Maryland.

The complainant initially asserted a claim of reprisal based on prior Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) activity; however, this reprisal allegation was voluntarily withdrawn during a pre-hearing conference conducted before the EEOC Administrative Judge assigned to the matter.
## CHRONOLOGY OF EVENTS
The complaint encompasses six distinct incidents spanning an eighteen-month period:

**First Instance - May through July 2018:** On three separate occasions (May 31, 2018; July 3, 2018; and July 16, 2018), the complainant's first-level supervisor, a Force Development Flight Chief with civil service rank GS-0301-13, asserted that verbal counseling had been administered to the complainant.
Notably, despite these claimed counseling sessions, no written documentation was generated or placed in the complainant's official personnel file.
**Second Instance - October 2018:** On October 18, 2018, the first-level supervisor issued a formal Letter of Reprimand to the complainant.

**Third Instance - February through April 2019:** Between February 12, 2019, and April 3, 2019, across five separate dates (February 12, March 14, March 21, April 2, and April 3), the first-level supervisor received and accepted statements from the complainant's direct subordinates that the complainant characterized as factually inaccurate, without conducting independent verification or supplemental investigation.
**Fourth Instance - April 2019:** On April 25, 2019, the complainant was furnished a Notice of Proposed Removal letter, formally signed by the first-level supervisor.
**Fifth Instance - June 2019:** Approximately June 28, 2019, the complainant received a Decision to Remove letter, also dated June 28, 2019, and bearing the signature of the first-level supervisor.
This letter effected the complainant's termination from federal service.

**Sixth Instance - October 2019:** On October 22, 2019, the complainant discovered that her Common Access Card (CAC), required for facility access and system authorization, remained in active status despite her removal from the Agency's payroll and employment.
This posed a security concern, as the active credentials could theoretically permit unauthorized individuals to access systems and modify the complainant's work files without authorization.
## INVESTIGATION CONCLUSION AND ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS

Upon completing the investigation, the Agency furnished the complainant with a copy of the investigative report and provided formal notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge.
The complainant timely requested such a hearing.

Despite the complainant's objections and contrary to her preference for a full evidentiary hearing, the assigned Administrative Judge granted the Agency's motion for summary judgment and issued a decision without conducting a hearing.
In this decision, the Administrative Judge determined that the complainant had failed to establish discrimination based on race, sex, color, or age.
The Agency subsequently issued a final order implementing the Administrative Judge's findings in their entirety.
The complainant subsequently filed an appeal of this decision.
## ADMINISTRATIVE JUDGE'S FINDINGS
The Administrative Judge's analysis proceeded from the principle that all facts presented in the investigation report would be viewed most favorably to the complainant.

Nevertheless, the Administrative Judge concluded that the complainant failed to establish a genuine issue of material fact sufficient to support discrimination claims based on any protected class status.

**Note on Claim Six:** Although the Administrative Judge technically addressed the complaint regarding the active CAC status as part of the overall decision, the complainant did not include this claim in her appellate brief and did not dispute the Administrative Judge's finding on this matter.
Consequently, Claim Six was not addressed in subsequent appellate review.
## ANALYSIS OF REMAINING CLAIMS

**Claims 1, 2, and 3 (Disciplinary Actions):** Regarding the undocumented verbal counseling, Letter of Reprimand, and acceptance of unverified subordinate statements, the Administrative Judge found that the complainant could not demonstrate disparate treatment or discriminatory harassment.
An Agency Human Resources officer affirmed in her sworn statement that verbal counseling is not required to be documented in personnel files under Agency policy.

**Claims 4 and 5 (Proposed Removal and Termination):** Assuming arguendo that the complainant could establish a prima facie case of discrimination regarding these claims, the Administrative Judge found that the Agency had articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for removal.

The first-level supervisor's stated basis for the termination decision included: failure to meet operational deadlines, unauthorized cancellation of scheduled events, inadequate schedule management to serve patron needs, failure to provide staff break and lunch relief, absence of formal staff planning meetings, employee allegations of gossip and disclosure of confidential personnel information, staff reports expressing fear of retaliation for speaking candidly, and inadequate attention to detail in financial management.
The complainant was unable to identify similarly situated employees who received more favorable treatment.

The complainant referenced coworkers who were not disciplined for an altercation occurring in front of patrons; however, the Administrative Judge rejected this comparison, noting that the coworkers held different positions and faced entirely different circumstances and conduct violations than the complainant.
**Hostile Work Environment Claims:** The Administrative Judge analyzed whether the complainant established harassment based on protected characteristics.

The complainant's hostile work environment allegations centered on: the undocumented verbal counseling referenced in the removal notice, the Letter of Reprimand regarding an unattended library, the acceptance of allegedly inaccurate statements from non-minority subordinates, and the removal and termination itself.
The Administrative Judge determined that the complainant failed to establish a nexus between these incidents and protected class status.
With respect to age and sex, the Administrative Judge found insufficient evidence beyond the complainant's conclusory statements.
Regarding race and color, the Administrative Judge concluded that speculation based solely on racial composition did not demonstrate racial animus.
An affidavit from a supporting coworker referenced unnamed staff members allegedly expressing preference for non-minority supervision and comparisons favoring the complainant's Caucasian predecessor.

However, the Administrative Judge found this affidavit unreliable, noting that the affiant apparently obtained this information indirectly rather than through personal observation, and that no corroborating evidence substantiated these allegations.
The Administrative Judge further determined that the complainant failed to establish severe and pervasive harassment that altered the conditions of employment into an abusive environment.

The events described constituted ordinary workplace interactions, including supervisory disagreements, management decisions, communication issues, and progressive disciplinary implementation rather than unlawful harassment.

The events described constituted ordinary workplace interactions, including supervisory disagreements, management decisions, communication issues, and progressive disciplinary implementation rather than unlawful harassment.
# INVESTIGATION CASE FILE RECORD
## CASE SUMMARY AND BACKGROUND
This case involves allegations of employment discrimination filed by a Contract Specialist at the Grade-11 level (GS-11) employed at the Agency's facility located in Gallup, New Mexico.

On August 25, 2015, the Complainant initiated formal proceedings by filing an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint with the Agency, alleging unlawful discrimination based on multiple protected characteristics and status.
Specifically, the complaint asserted discrimination based on race (Native American), national origin (Native American), age, and alleged retaliation for engaging in protected EEO activity.

The Agency accepted the formal complaint for investigation by letter dated November 23, 2015, thereby initiating the investigative process required under applicable federal employment discrimination statutes and regulations.

Following completion of the investigation, the Agency provided the Complainant with copies of the investigative report and formal notice of her statutory right to request a hearing before an Administrative Judge (AJ) of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC).
In accordance with her rights under the applicable regulatory framework, the Complainant timely requested an administrative hearing on her claims.
## ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS
The assigned Administrative Judge granted the Agency's motion for summary judgment decision without holding a hearing, despite objections raised by the Complainant.
This motion was filed on March 22, 2018, and the AJ issued her summary judgment decision on September 23, 2020, approximately two years following the motion filing.
The AJ's decision addressed twenty distinct claims of discrimination and retaliation, each involving specific employment actions allegedly taken against the Complainant between May 2015 and May 2018.
## ENUMERATED CLAIMS

The Administrative Judge systematically framed the allegations as follows: Claims 1 and 5 involved denials of Federal Acquisition Certification-Contracting (FAC-C) Level II training and certification occurring on May 15, June 3, and September 10, 2015, respectively.
Claims 2 and 6 addressed how these training denials purportedly impaired the Complainant's ability to qualify for advancement and promotion opportunities.
Claims 3 through 4, 7 through 8, and 10 through 11 involved non-selection for various contract specialist positions at multiple grade levels across several geographic locations and time periods.
The FAC-C program, referenced throughout the proceedings, establishes education, experience, and training standards applicable to the federal government acquisition workforce.

Additional claims addressed the non-renewal of the Complainant's FAC-C certification and warrant on April 4, 2016 (Claim 9); non-referral for position opportunities (Claim 11); alleged harassment involving unwanted physical contact by an Agency officer designated as C1 occurring on May 2, 2016 (Claim 12); denial of permission to attend contract administration training scheduled for April 24, 2017 through May 5, 2017 (Claim 18); and delays in approval of leave requests from April 18, 2017 through May 4, 2018, with approvals made contingent upon completion of specified work assignments (Claim 19).
The final claim alleged that the Agency informed the Complainant she could not obtain a Level II FAC-C warrant without approval from the Bureau Procurement Chief, identified as C1 (Claim 20).
## ADMINISTRATIVE JUDGE'S FINDINGS
The Administrative Judge's analysis resulted in findings of no discrimination or retaliation across the majority of claims.
Regarding Claim 8, the AJ determined that the Complainant failed to establish even a prima facie case of discrimination because she had not submitted an application for the position in question.

For Claims 3, 4, 7, 11, 13, and 16, the AJ found that the Complainant lacked the minimum qualifications for these positions, specifically because she did not possess the required Level II and Level III FAC-C certifications.
With respect to Claim 14, the AJ noted that the selected candidate shared the same national origin and gender as the Complainant and was older in age.
Additionally, the AJ found no evidence that the selecting official was aware of the Complainant's prior EEO activity, thereby undermining any inference of retaliation.

Regarding Claims 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 15, 17, 18, 19, and 20, the AJ determined that the Agency had articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions and that the Complainant had failed to demonstrate these reasons were pretextual.
Concerning Claim 12, involving the alleged unwanted physical contact, the AJ noted that the Complainant had not characterized the contact as possessing sexual aspects.

The AJ concluded that no evidence demonstrated that the Complainant's protected class status motivated the physical contact and that a single incident, even if unwelcome, was insufficient to establish a hostile work environment.
## FINAL ORDER AND APPEAL

The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting in its entirety the Administrative Judge's findings and conclusions, determining that the Complainant had failed to prove the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.
This final order prompted the instant appeal.
## APPELLANT'S CONTENTIONS
On appeal, through counsel, the Complainant advances several arguments.
She contends that the Agency has engaged in systematic denial of promotions to qualified Native Americans.

The Complainant asserts that the Agency official designated C1 determined that a seventeen-hour class on analyzing contract costs was insufficient for Level II certification, despite another Agency official's approval of that training.

She further contends that C1 unilaterally decided, without Office of Personnel Management approval, that future contracting positions would require Level II certification, allegedly to reduce hiring of Native Americans.
Regarding Claim 10, the Complainant argues the Agency failed to articulate any legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for its action.

Concerning the unwanted physical contact allegation (Claim 12), the Complainant provides alternative characterization, suggesting that C1's embrace could support an inference of implicit bias, arguing the conduct reflects an attitude viewing Native American women as inferior individuals unworthy of professional respect.
## AGENCY RESPONSE
The Agency requests affirmation of the final order implementing the Administrative Judge's decision, maintaining that no discrimination occurred and requesting dismissal of all claims.

# INVESTIGATION CASE FILE RECORD
**CASE SUMMARY AND BACKGROUND**
During the relevant period, the Complainant served as a Senior Special Agent and Polygraph Examiner within the Forensic Services Division located in Washington, D.C.

On January 2, 2020, the Complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging that the Agency engaged in discriminatory practices and retaliation in response to previously protected EEO activity.
The Agency accepted the formal complaint for investigation by letter dated March 11, 2020, and identified three distinct claims for adjudication.
**CLAIMS AND ALLEGATIONS**
The first claim addressed whether the Complainant received a lower Supervisory Evaluation (SE) rating on his 2019 Merit Promotion Plan compared to his previous supervisor's 2018 rating.

The second claim alleged a discriminatory hostile work environment based on retaliation, encompassing three subclaims: (a) that on or about September 10, 2019, a supervisory official identified as [S2] obstructed the Complainant's return to Quality Control and mentor duties; (b) that on or about September 13, 2019, [S2] denied the Complainant's request for reconsideration regarding these duties; and (c) that since September 1, 2019, [S2] and another Agency official delegated assignments directly to Washington Field Office examiners while excluding the Complainant from communications, thereby circumventing his role as Senior Polygraph Examiner and Polygraph Backup.
**AGENCY'S INVESTIGATION AND INITIAL DECISION**
Following its investigation, the Agency provided the Complainant with a copy of the investigation report and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge.
The Agency subsequently issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination.
Regarding the first claim, the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the Supervisory Evaluation rating.
For subclaims 2(a) and 2(b), the Agency maintained that the Complainant had been restored to mentoring duties and remained under consideration for Quality Control duties.
Concerning subclaim 2(c), the Agency reported that [S2] denied consulting with the Complainant or excluding him from communications.
**COMPLAINANT'S APPEAL ARGUMENTS**
The Complainant appealed the Agency's final decision, raising several contentions.
He asserted that the Agency issued an untimely final decision, claiming he submitted his request for a final decision on July 10, 2020, and requested a default judgment sanction.
The Complainant further argued that the Report of Investigation was inadequate and contended that his 2019-2020 Supervisory Evaluation represented a continuation of alleged retaliatory conduct.
He highlighted that three months prior to receiving his Supervisory Evaluation, he had received an "Outstanding" rating on his annual performance appraisal.

Additionally, the Complainant asserted that less qualified employees were selected for mentoring and quality control duties, that one management official failed to respond to testimony requests, and that the Agency had not complied with a previous final decision ordering his reassignment to Quality Control and EEO training for specified management officials.
**AGENCY'S RESPONSE**
The Agency responded that the Merit Promotion Plan Supervisory Evaluation constitutes a separate and distinct process from annual performance evaluations.
The Agency noted that [S2] had not completed the Complainant's 2018-2019 Supervisory Evaluation.

Regarding the collateral duties, the Agency confirmed the Complainant's approval to resume mentoring duties and stated he remains eligible for Quality Control duties, subject to various selection factors.
Concerning the alleged communication exclusion, the Agency asserted that the Complainant received treatment consistent with other examiners.
The Agency further argued that any delay in issuing the final decision was minimal and did not warrant sanctions.
